subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Whereas the Imperial conference of 1923 recommended for the acceptance of the governments of the empire represented that the following procedure should be observed in the negotiation, signature and ratification of international agreements:
The word "treaty" is used in the sense of an agreement which, in accordance with the normal practice of diplomacy, would take the form of a treaty between heads of states, signed by plenipotentiaries provided with full powers issued by the heads of the states, and authorizing the holders to conclude a treaty.

1.	Negotiation.
(a)	It is desirable that no treaty should be negotiated by any of the governments of the empire without due consideration of its possible effect on other parts of the empire, or, if circumstances so demand, on the empire as a whole.
(b)	Before negotiations are opened with the intention of concluding a treaty, steps should be taken to ensure that any of the other governments of the empire likely to be interested are informed, so that, if any such government considers that its interests would be affected it may have an opportunity of expressing its views, or, when it3 interests are intimately involved, of participating in the negotiations.
(c)	In all cases where more than one of the governments of the empire participates in the negotiations, there should be the fullest possible exchange of views between those governments before and during the negotiations. In the case of treaties negotiated at international conferences, where there is a British Empire delegation, on which, in accordance with the, now established practice the dominions and India are separately represented, such representation should also be utilized to attain this object.	.
(d)	Steps should be taken to ensure that those governments of the empire whose representatives are not participating in the negotiations should, during their progress, be kept informed in regard to any points arising in which they may be interested.
2.	Signature.
(a)	Bilateral treaties imposing obligations on one part of the empire only should be signed by a representative of the government of that part of the empire in respect of which the obligations are to be undertaken, and the preamble and text of the treaty should be worded as to make its scope clear.
(b)	Where a bilateral treaty imposes obligations on more than one part of the empire, the treaty should be signed by one or more plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments concerned.
(c)	As regards treaties negotiated at international conferences, the existing practice of signature by plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments of the empire represented at the conference should be continued, and the full powers should be in the form employed at Paris and Washington.
3.	Ratification.
The existing practice in connection with the ratification of treaties should be maintained.

Apart from treaties made between heads of states, it is not unusual for agreements to be made between governments. Such agreements, which are usually of

International Agreements
a technical or administrative character, are made in the names of the signatory governments, and signed by representatives of those governments, who do not act under full powers issued by the heads of the states: they are not ratified by the heads of the states, though in some cases some form of acceptance or confirmation by the governments concerned is employed. As regards agreements of this nature the existing practice should be continued, but before entering on negotiations the governments of the empire should consider whether the interests of any other part of the empire may be affected, and, if so, steps should be taken to ensure that the government of such part is informed of the proposed negotiations, in order that it may have an opportunity of expressing its views.
And whereas it was further agreed that the existing procedure in relation to ratification of treaties was as follows:
(a)	The ratification of treaties imposing obligations on one part of the empire is effected at the instance of the government of that part:
(b)	The ratification of treaties imposing obligations on more than one part of the empire is effected after consultation between the governments of those parts of the empire concerned. It is for each government to decide whether parliamentary approval or legislation is required before desire for, or concurrence in, ratification is intimated by that government.
This House approves of the procedure proposed for the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties and conventions, and considers further that before His Majesty's Canadian ministers advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of anj' treaty convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
He said:	The resolution which you have
just reald, Mr. Speaker, relates to the all important question of the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties involving military or economic sanctions. The resolution will be founid to divide itself into two parts, the first part asking formal approval by parliament of the resolution respecting the negotiation, signature and' ratification of treaties which was adopted at the Imperial conference of 1923; the second part asking the approval by parliament of the procedure to be adopted with respect to the ratification of treaties only upon the prior approval by parliament which, under the resolution of the Imperial conference, was left optional with the different governments and parliaments of the empire concerned. My reason for bringing this resolution forward1 at this time is that another Imperial conference has been called' to assemble in London in October of this year. It is, I think, desirable that representatives of the government attending that conference should be in a position to state that the parliament of Canada has approved the resolution respecting the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties which was adopted at the previous conference. I think it desirable also that the House and the Imperial conference should know the attitude which the representatives of the government will be expected to take in 14011-302
stating the position of this country on the all important matter of procedure with respect to the ratification of treaties.
In connection with the first part of this resolution I assume there will be very little if any question as to the attitude of parliament. Indeed, I hope the entire resolution will meet with the unanimous approval of this House, and: if I refrain from going into matters of possible controversy it is because of a desire to have agreement between all parties in this House as far as possible in connection with these questions which relate to our interimperial and international relations. The resolution considered in a broad way is one which should commend itself to all groups in this parliament; at any rate it is my hope that the discussion will so resolve itself.
In connection with the first part of the resolution requesting approval by parliament of the resolution adopted at the Imperial conference of 1923 respecting the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties, I would say that at the Imperial conference this resolution was unanimously approved by the governments represented there. It was approved by the government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and by the representatives of the governments of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Newfoundland and the Irish Free State and Canada, as well as by the representatives of India. In the circumstances, therefolre, I think there will be little difficulty in finding general acceptance of the resolution in this parliament. It may, however, be advisable to put on record the reference made in the report of the Imperial conference itself as to the manner in which a decision was reached with respect to this particular resolution.
I might anticipate the reading of that particular paragraph by recalling to the House the discussion which we had in this parliament in a previous session with respect to the negotiation of a treaty with the United States having to do with the conservation of the halibut resources on the Pacific coast. Hon. members present at that' time will recall that the government of the day, the present administration, took the view that as that treaty affected only this part of the empire and related to a matter of mutual concern to the great republic to the south and ourselves, it was right and proper that the negotiations should be conducted by ministers of the crown representing the government of Canada, and that the ministers so conducting the negotiations should be given full powers by His Majesty, and that the same rights which existed with respect to the negotiation of the treaty should also exist with re-

International Agreements

spect to its signature and with respect also to its ratification. In other words, that as it was a treaty which concerned only one part of the empire, the part of the empire alone concerned was the part which should undertake and carry through the negotiations and advise ratification.
The consideration of the Halibut treaty gave rise, as I have said, tQ some discussion in parliament and to a difference in the point of view as between the parties as to whether the government in thus asserting Canada's position was perhaps not going too far in placing upon the shoulders of its ministers obligations which theretofore had been exercised by either ambassadors or ministers of the home government. There was a considerable discussion here, considerable discussion in the press of this country and in the Old Country as to the whole position, the significance being as to whether or not it marked a departure in the negotiation of treaties. That was how the matter came to come before the Imperial conference.
I shall not go into the discussions which took place at the Imperial conference with respect to that matter. All I wish to say to the House at the moment is that the Canadian position as taken was maintained absolutely by the Imperial conference as a whole. Not only did the ministers of the other self-governing dominions take the position, in giving their assent to the resolution, that what Canada had done with respect to that particular treaty was done in a right and proper way, but the conference went further and said that with respect to similar classes of treaties in the future the procedure there adopted should be the one to be followed.
In considering the question of the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties, a special committee of the conference was appointed to give the matter detailed study. That special committee was presided over by the late Lord Curzon, who at the time was Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and it had the advice and assistance of the able counsel of the Foreign Office, Sir Cecil Hurst. The record of the 'proceedings of the conference will be found on page 13 of the Summary of Proceedings presented to His Majesty's parliament in November, 1923, as follows:
The principles governing the relations of the various parts of the empire in connection with the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties seemed to the conference to be of the greatest importance. Accordingly it was arranged that the subject should be fully examined by a committee, of which the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs was chairman. The Secretary of State for the Colonies, the Prime Ministers of Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, New Zealand,

the Union of South Africa and Newfoundland, the Minister of External Affairs of the Irish Free State, and the Secretary of State for India as head of the Indian Delegation, served on this committee. With the assistance of the legal adviser to the Foreign Office, Sir C. J. B. Hurst, K.C.B., K.C., the following resolution was drawn up and agreed to:

The full power issued to such representative should indicate the part of empire in respect of which the obligations are to be undertaken, and the preamble and text of the treaty should be so worded as to make its scope clear.
"(b) Where a bilateral treaty imposes obligations on more than one part of the empire, the treaty should be signed by one or more plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments concerned.
"(c) As regards treaties negotiated at international conferences, the existing practice of signature by plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments of the empire represented at the conference should be continued, and the full powers should be in the form employed at Paris and Washington.
"3. Ratification.
"The existing practice in connection with the ratification of treaties should be maintained."
That is part I of the resolution. Hon. members will notice that the House is asked

International Agreements
to approve of the procedure proposed for the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties and conventions as set forth in that resolution. As I say, I think there can be no possibility of the House in any way taking exception to the form of procedure as therein outlined. I would only add this, that since this resolution of the Imperial conference was adopted, the government has proceeded in the negotiation of other treaties upon the basis therein laid down. In the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for the year ending March 1, 1925, which was tabled in the House at the beginning of this session, will be found a list of the treaties that have been negotiated, signed and ratified since this resolution went into effect.
I have already spoken of the Halibut treaty, which has been signed and ratified prior to the meeting of the Imperial conference. The next treaty to be negotiated, signed and ratified in accordance with the proceedings therein set forth was the commercial treaty with Belgium. I might say, in passing, with respect to the signature of that treaty that it was the first treaty in the history of the Dominion to be signed in Canada by Canadian ministers of the crown holding full powers from His Majesty to sign in his name. The first treaty of the kind to be signed in Carlada; the Halibut treaty, had been signed by ministers, of the crown of Canada holding full power from his Majesty to sign in his name, but it was signed at Washington, and not at Ottawa,. The commercial treaty with Belgium has the historic significance of 'being the first treaty approved by this parliament, negotiated and signed in Canada, with the full powers given by His Majesty to Canadian ministers to act on his behalf.
The other treaties with the United States which were signed since the resolution of the Imperial conference are the- convention for the purposes of suppressing smuggling operations along the international boundary, and preventing the violation of the laws regarding narcotics, which was signed at Washington on June 6, 1924, and ratifications exchanged at the same place on July 17, 1925. A supplementary convention to provide for extradition on account of crimes against the laws for the suppression of traffic in narcotics was signed at Washington on January 8, 1925. and ratifications were exchanged on July 17, 1925. On February 24, 1925, a convention between Canada and the United States was signed at Washington providing for the regulation of the levels of the lake of the Woods, ratifications being duly exchanged at Washington on July 17, 1925.
At Washington on the same day a treaty was signed to define more accurately the international boundary between the two countries, and ratifications were exchanged at Washington on July 17, 1925.
Hon. members will find in this report references to other conventions and treaties, some of them of a. commercial character and some relating more particularly to negotiations between different parts of the British Empire. But the treaties which I have just mentioned are treaties with foreign countries, treaties which were negotiated by Canadan ministers holding full power from His Majesty for the purpose and signed by them in the name of His Majesty, and the ratification of which was effected after this parliament had approved of the treaties. So, Mr. Speaker, I submit that with respect to the first part of the resolution which sets forth t)he procedure to be followed in regard to negotiation, signature and ratification, this parliament may be assumed by its repeated actions to have endorsed the resolution in full, and there should therefore be no difficulty at the present time in obtaining formal approval of the course of procedure there outlined.
The second part of the resolution asks the approval of parliament to one particular form of procedure with respect to the ratification of the treaties. May I pause here to remind hon. members that ratification of a treaty is an executive act-it is an act of the sovereign. Sometimes in the discussion of these international questions we use terminology with a freedom that is perhaps hardly permissible if we wish to be exact, and not infrequently one hears mention of a treaty being ratified by parliament. The act of ratification is an executive act, an act performed by the sovereign. It is performed by the sovereign, however, on the advice df his ministers, that may be regarded as sufficient, or there may be a limitation placed upon ministers before advising ratification-such a limitation as is suggested in the present resolution, namely of approval by the parliament of the country in the first instance. In the resolution of the Imperial conference it was stated that the procedure with respect to ratification was to remain as it had existed theretofore. That meant that it was optional with the parliaments or the governments of the different countries concerned to decide whether or not ratification should be on the advice of the ministry solely, or whether it should be upon the approval of parliament in the first instance. The present government, jn the case of Canada, believes that it will help to avoid embarrassments and dissensions, that it will make

International Agreements

for greater unity and for greater security with-dn the empire in the long run, if the general practice is adopted with respect to important treaties such as involve military and economic sanctions of approval by parliament Of such treaties in the first instance preceding advice on the part of the ministry favourable to ratification.

come up at the Imperial conference, and I would like to be in a position, should it be my privilege to present to parliament matters connected with the Locarno agreement, to give all those phases careful study and investigation before pronouncing too definitely upon them. But what I wish to direct the attention of the House to at the moment is that clause 9 of the treaty of mutual guarantee as it stands at present reads:	-
The present treaty shall impose no obligation upon any of the British dominions, or upon India, unless the government of such dominion, or of India, signifies its acceptance thereof.
Some critics who have, examined the treaty have been inclined to be suspicious of the use of the word "government", rather than the use of the word "parliament", as it appeared in a previous treaty of guarantee relating more particularly to France, which was proposed a couple of years ago, but which did not become .effective. In that treaty, a treaty of guarantee, to which the United States, France and Britain were named as -parties, and1 which contained provision similar to the one now found in the Locarno treaty, it was stated that the treaty would impose no obligation upon the dominion unless the parliament of such dominion signified its acceptance thereof. The use of the word "government" in the present Locarno agreement would seem to suggest that in the minds of those who had to do with the drafting of the treaty there was a reason why the word "parliament" should be dropped and the word "government" substituted therefor. May I say that, after knowing, as I do from the correspondence, what was in the mind, of the British government, I have no hesitation in saying that the British government had no ulterior object in view, so far as the change of the word "parliament" to "government" was concerned. This clause, as hon. members will notice, speaks of India as well as the dominions. India has not a parliament in a position to express approval on matters of this kind, and I believe that was the consideration which governed in the use of the word "government" in this clause rather than the word "parliament." But what the British government itself has anticipated, what it expects at the present time, is that before Canada becomes a party to the Locarno agreement, this parliament will be asked to express its approval. It is not anticipated that the government regardless of parliament will be expected to give approval on the part of Canada. That, I think, is sufficient with respect to the Locarno agreement.

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION

speechtext:
My hon. friend could not have been listening. I did tell the House. I said that up to the present time the government had not seen any reason why it should assume obligations under this par-

International Agreements
ticular clause which leaves it optional for the dominions to say whether or not they will assume these obligations.
In conclusion I have just one other word to say bearing directly on this matter. Hon. members will have noticed that I have drawn a distinction between an obligation placed upon a government and an obligation placed upon parliament. In this instance I direct my present remarks more in the form of a question to the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) than of any observations with respect to certain declarations which he has made on the subject of Canada's participation in foreign wars which, of course, arises out of obligations assumed through agreements, treaties or conventions.
In a speech made at Hamilton in the fall of last year my right hon. friend is reported as making a very significant statement, I hope he will correct me if in any particular I fail to give the quotation aright. I am taking the following quotation from my right hon. friend's speech as it is found reported in the Mail and Empire of Toronto, of November 17, special to the Mail and Empire from the staff reporter at Hamilton under date of November 16. I will not attempt to read the whole of the speech, but I will deal with the point that is pertinent to my present remarks. My right hon. friend is reported as saying:
If ever the time should come when the spectre of 1914 should again appear I believe it would be best not only that parliament should be called, but that the decision of the government which, of course, would have to be given promptly, should be submitted to the judgment of the people at a general election before troops should leave our shores. This would contribute to the unity of our country in the months to come and would enable us best to do our duty. It would not mean delay. Under the stress of war delay would be fatal. Let me make clear what I mean. The government would have to decide and decide quickly what was best in the interests of Canada. The government would have to act on its judgment, but before there was anything in the way of participation involving the despatch of troops the will of the people of Canada should first be obtained.
The question I wish to ask my right hon. friend is this-and I hope he will explain it when he gets up to speak-whether by that declaration he means that it shall rest solely with the government to make the decision whether or not Canada shall participate in wars or whether it shall be parliament which must approve before the further 3 p.m. reference is made to the people as a whole in a general election. As I read my right hon. friend's remarks they are capable of two interpretations. One is that if Canada is asked to participate in a war parliament will be summoned, but there
is no obligation to place before parliament for its approval the decision taken with respect to sending troops overseas. I think my right hon. friend's remarks may be read to mean that the government itself, irrespective of parliament, will have the deters mination of whether or not troops are to go overseas; what the government would do would be to call parliament together very quickly and as soon as parliament is called together there will be an appeal from parliament to the people in a general election after the government has reached a decision but _ before it has submitted its decision to parliament for approval.

Mr. MACKENZIE KIN|G:	Well, Mr. Speaker, I direct the attention of the House and the country to the tactics of my right hon. friend at the present moment. I will read the 'language again so that hon. members will see his position exactly. He said:

-but before there was anything in the way of participation involving the despatch of troops the will of the people of Canada should first be obtained.

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext: We are not children.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I have no
desire to geit into a controversy in this matter. As I said at the beginning, I only wish to state the position in the clearest, possible way. I asked my right hon. friend for an explanation, of the words which he used, but I have not yet been able to get from him an explanation which the country will regard as satisfactory. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the position of the present administration and of the Liberal party, that whate'ver may be the position of my right hon. friend and of those who surround him, on this grave question of the obligation of the country to participate in foreign wars, we declare that in regard to the ratification of treaties, conventions or agreements involving military or economic sanctions we stand first, last and always for approval in the first instance by the parliament of Canada. We do not take the extreme of ignoring parliament in one way or the other. We believe that parliament stands as the one body representative of the nation as a whole, and we believe that by having it understood in advance that on all these great questions parliament will be consulted and its approval obtained, we will be helping to maintain without possibility of division or difference

International Agreements
the relations between the different parts of this great empire, and that in the most effective way we will be able to further unity within our own country and unity within the British Empire as well.
Mr. C. H. CA'HAN:	(St. Lawrence-St.
George):	Mr. Speaker, the resolution which
the Prime Minister has placed before the House embodies, as I understand it, the existing practice with regard to the ratification of treaties in so far as they are ratified, or in so far as signification is given of their ratification, on behalf of the Canadian dominion. The resolution in itself consists of two parts. First, it approves of certain procedure proposed for the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties and conventions affecting Canada. I do not understand that there is anything new in this procedure. Secondly, it affirms as a rule of public .policy that before the government of Canada shall advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement, involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should first be obtained.
Now, dealing with the first part of this resolution, I understand that the duly authorized representatives of the Canadian government may, in accordance with its terms, properly sign treaties or conventions on behalf of Canada without having received the .prior authority of the .parliament of Canada to do so, but that no such treaty or convention or agreement so signed shall be binding upon Canada until it has been formally approved by the parliament of Canada. The preamble to the resolution also affirms that no treaty shalll be signed on behalf of one part of the empire which shall affect any other part, without affording to any and every other part, which is likely to be interested, full opportunity to be heard, and when the interests of that other part are intimately involved, opportunity to participate in the negotiations. Such provisions are reasonable and I think undoubtedly in accordance with the existing practice. As to the ratification of such treaties or conventions, the preamble to the resolution affirms that the said practice or procedure should be maintained, and the existing procedure is declared to be as follows:
(a)	the ratification of treaties imposing obligations on one part of the empire is effected at the instance of the government of that part.
(b)	the ratification of treaties imposing obligations on more than one part of the empire is effected after consultation between the governments of those parts of the empire concerned.
But I call the attention of the Prime Minister particularly to this fact, that neither
the preamble to the resolution nor the resolution itself declares that no such treaty or convention shall be binding on a self-governing dominion of the empire except it be accepted by the government of that dominion.
In other words, in the treaty of Locarno, as the Prime Minister stated, under article 9 it is provided that the present treaty shall impose no obligation upon any of the British dominions or upon India unless the government of such dominion or of India shall signify its acceptance thereof. First, I would ask the Prime Minister was it the clear understanding at the Imperial conference of 1923 that hereafter no treaty or convention negotiated by the crown should be binding upon the Dominion of Canada or the other dominions unless its ratification were assented to or signified by the government, subject of course in the case of Canada to the approval of. the Canadian parliament? Are we not to understand that up to this date there have been many treaties entered into by the crown which undoubtedly bind Canada, even although the Canadian government has not intimated its assent or acceptance and even although the Canadian parliament has not been called upon to approve the same? Is this a new departure? Is it clearly understood that hereafter the crown,-because it is the crown alone that can negotiate treaties- shall not negotiate any treaty or convention which shall apply to or bind Canada or which, in the words of the resolution, shall affect Canada without such treaty being assented to by the government based in the ease of Canada, if this resolution is in force and the prior practice prevails, upon the authority of this parliament? Would the hon. gentleman answer now, or shall I wait until later?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I cannot see
that there is any occasion for the resolution at all unless the language means that where one part of the empire is affected, that part in order to be bound must be kept advised of the negotiations, and must be a signatory and agree to ratification of the treaty in question.

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext: Then I understand that this is a new departure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I would not
say that; I am rather inclined to believe that what has been set out in the resolution is what has been assumed in the past despite such different views as others may have held. Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and all the Prime Ministers of this country have I believe taken the view that Canada is not necessarily bound by treaties signed without her knowledge and without her consent.
International Agreements

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Then I understand that the
resolution makes it clear that the understanding approved by the representatives at the Imperial conference is, then, that hereafter the crown will refrain from making any treaty applicable to and binding on any one of the dominions unless with the assent of the government of that dominion, leaving it to that government and its parliament to decide as to whether prior to the consent of the government being given, there shall be express approval by the parliament of that dominion.
There is another point as to the ratification of any treaty or convention by the government of Canada. The resolution provides generally that the approval of the Canadian parliament must first be obtained, but the terms of the resolution seem to me to discriminate between a treaty or convention affecting Canada which may be ratified on notification by the Canadian government, and a treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions to which the government of Canada may signify its acceptance. I would like to ask the Prime Minister if this is a mere matter of a little irregular drafting, or whether by the use of the different words, a treaty or convention affecting Canada in the one place, and, in the other, a treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanction, the one term is intended to be exclusive of the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I am very,
glad my hon. friend has asked that question. As the resolution was originally drafted and placed on the order paper it read, I think, "Any treaty or convention affecting Canada." As I studied that language it appeared to me to be broad enough to include treaties of a purely technical and administrative character.
I did not wish the resolution to go that far; I did not wish to ask that all treaties of a purely technical or administrative character should necessarily come before parliament for approval. What I wished to make clear however, was that all treaties or conventions involving military or economic sanctions must come before parliament, and where military or economic sanctions were involved I wished to make the terms broad enough to include agreements, so that in referring to treaties or agreements of any kind we would not have a difference over the mere use of words.

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I would suggest that the
resolution might be made clearer if it stated, "any treaty affecting Canada and particularly any treaty involving military or economic

sanctions." It also strikes me that there is some discrepancy in the last few words of the resolution:
-or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
I can well understand that the approval of parliament might be "secured" by a majority of the members sitting behind the Prime Minister agreeing in terms to support a particular treaty upon the calling of parliament. In that way it would be secured within the meaning of that w'ord, but I would suggest that a better word would be "obtained". That is a far better wofd, but I do not wish to be technical.
Although this resolution may and probably does, as the Prime Minister says, embody only the existing procedure, as far back as I can remember, over thirty or forty years, no treaty has been negotiated by or on behalf of Canada which has not been subject to the approval of parliament before it belcame effective. In that respect I am entirely at one with the Prime Minister in upholding the supremacy of the Canadian parliament in dealing with matters directly affecting Canada and the Canadian people. In reading again Lord Durham's report of 1839, I chanced to come upon the vivid and inspiring message which he sent to the British colonies of North America:
If in the hidden decrees of that wisdom 'by which this world is ruled, it is written that these countries are not forever to remain portions of the empire, we owe it to our honour to take good care that, when they separate from us. they should not be the only countries on the American continent in which the Anglo-Saxon race shall be found unfit to govern itself.
I think in dealing with all these matters of inter-imperial and external affairs the sooner is is clearly recognized, not only by the people but by members of this parliament as well, that the future destiny of this country rests in the hands of the men who sit in parliament representing the people, the sooner will we have a clear consciousness of the grave responsibilities which Test upon parliament in dealing with all matters of this character. I remember well in my native province of Nova Scotia when every boy of my age was taught to read at college the discussions from 1839 to 1846 in our own provincial parliament, dluring that memorable contest for responsible selfgovernment in Nova Scotia in which the late Hon. Joseph Howe took such an important lead. I remember hearing him speak once myself, though but a lad, on these matters, and in the whole eastern part of Canada there was left an indelible impression upon the minds of the electorate, which exists even to this day, that in all matters of domestic and internal policy

International Agreements
the parliament of Canada must be supreme. Since that time there has grown up a strong, a seriously strong, impression that in all matters of external or inter-imperial policy affecting Canada, the parliament of Canada must have the decisive word, and therefore it is that I regard this expression, of the procedure that has gradually developed during the last thirty or forty years, embodied' in a resolution of this kind, as being somewhat impressive, although it does not incorporate any new principle of public policy.
But I suggest that so long ago as the discussion of the confederation resolutions, Sir John A. Macdonald anticipated some such possibility as this. I notice that in his oration upon the Quebec resolutions in 1865, he declared at great length that with respect to the future destiny of Canada, its political destiny, even if it be independence of the British Empire, the people and parliament of Canada must have the supreme and final decision, even in regard to independence, because I wish to impress the view that, if this country desires independence of the British Empire, parliament at the present time is perfectly free to declare what our political future shall be, and that decision will be supreme and binding and final so far as the British government is concerned. I have at my hand a dozen or more statements of that view from the most responsible statesmen of the British Empire, down through all the years from 1839 to the present. But the very fact that we have this power, the very fact that w:e have this authority, the very fact that the supreme decision rests with us as the representatives of the people in the House of Commons, places upon the government and places upon parliament a grave responsibility with regard to the exercise of these powers, even indirectly, and with regard sometimes to very trivial affairs. Sir John A. Macdonald said:
One argument, but not a strong one, has been urged against this confederation, that iit is an advance towards independence. Some are apprehensive that the very fact of our forming .this union will hasten the time when we shall (be severed from .the Mother Country. I have no apprehension of that kind. I believe it will have the contrary effect. I believe that as we grow stronger, thait as it is feLt dn England we 'have become a ipeople, able from our union, our strength, our population, and .the development of our resources, to take our position among the nations, she will be less willing to pant with us than she would Ibe now, when we are broken up into a number of 'insignificant colonies, subject ito attack piece-meal without any concerted action or common organization of defence.
I am strongly of opinion that year by year, as we grow in population and strength, England will more and more see the advantages of maintaining the alliance between British North America and herself. Does any one imagine that, when our population, instead of three and a half, will be seven millions, as it will be ere many years pass, we will be one whit more willing than now to sever the connection with England ? Would not these seven millions be just as anxious to maintain their allegiance to the queen and their connection with the Mother Countiy, as we are now? ....
And when by means of this rapid increase we become a nation of eight or nine millions of inhabitants, our alliance will be worthy of being sought by the great nations of the earth. I am proud to believe that our desire for a permanent alliance will be reciprocated in England	
The colonies are now in a transition state. Gradually a different colonial system is being developed- and it will become, year by year, less a case of dependence on our pant, and of over-ruling protection on- the .part of the Mother Country, and more a case of healthy and cordial alliance.
For myself, although I pray God may forbid that in this generation or in succeeding generations we shall be separated from the British crown or sever our allegiance to the British crown as it at present exists, I believe that it is absolutely necessary that the people of this country should thoroughly appreciate and understand1 that the political future of Canada that the destiny of this country is in their bands, and that we may have whatever future political career the great body of the people of Canada, as represented in this House of Commons, may decide to have for Canada. I believe in the necessity of maintaining the supremacy of the Canadian parliament in respect of all matters affecting the peace, progress and prosperity of Canada, but I believe also in the supreme necessity of creating in all sections of the Canadian people complete confidence in the efficiency and in the efficacy of our parliamentary institutions. If we fail in this Dominion of Canada to create and maintain such a confidence, all our institutions, which we have developed year after year and year after year during the last century, will fall to, pieces of their own weight. It is only by maintaining the confidence of the people of Canada in the good faith, in the efficiency, and in the efficacy of parliament, that we can maintain parliamentary institutions in this country. For parliamentary institutions, it seems to me there are only two alternatives-either communistic or autocratic despotism. There remain to-day in the whole wide world exercising the rights, the duties, and the responsibilities of democratic government those countries alone which have adopted and maintain English parliamentary institutions.
With regard to the matter to which the Prime Minister has alluded, I wish to say that it seems to me that when grave international crises arise, if they do arise, in the future history of this country, in which the political
International Agreements

security of the country is menaced, the parliament of Canada must take full responsibility for such immediate action as may be necessary to safeguard the public interest. I do not remember that in this country the principle of parliamentary responsibility in this respect has ever been directly questioned, and may we not, Mr. Speaker, have implicit confidence that in the future, as in the past, the representatives of the people sitting in this House of Commons will have sufficient courage and sufficient confidence to act up to the full measure of their responsibilities?
In case of such a crisis arising under exceptional circumstances when the House of Commons is more or less equally divided and when public opinion is doubtful, in order that the action or decision of parliament might not be rendered nugatory and ineffective a dissolution of parliament might be necessary, even for instance in such a great international crisis as that with which we were confronted in 1914. That may be possible, but as we know there is a discretion as to the dissolution of parliament vested in His Excellency the Governor General, and we have never yet had occasion to complain very much of the exercise of that discretion by the representatives of the crown who have held that high office in this country. But in the exercise of that discretion I personally hope that at no time will any representative of the crown precipitate an election when there are grave differences of opinion in this country, an election which would engender social disunion and civil strife, and possibly rioting and bloodshed in our midst, over a question of external or inter-imperial policy. The great safety of the empire lies in the fact that the crown, as represented by the British government, has left in the control and disposition of the governments and parliaments of each dominion the power to decide in all these matters of inter-imperial and external policy; and I think that we of this older generation, who have lived through times of crises and have lived nearer to the events of the period from 1835 to 1846, must have full confidence that the younger members in this House, who will be here long after we are gone, and others who are their successors, will be so imbued with a deep sense of the responsibility of the high offices they hold and of the grave trust which is confided to them as members of this House that in deciding upon these matters of inter-imperial or international importance they will so exercise their discretion and so render their decision as to compel the almost unanimous approval and support of every section of this vast and important Dominion.

It seems to me that the great danger at the present time in connection with our domestic affairs is the tendency in this country-I do not wish to be more specific-to separate in respect of inter-imperial and international affaire, and to create divisions of opinion with respect to those matters of external policy, which also serve to create dissensions in respect to the domestic policies of this country and prevent that unanimity and solidarity of opinion being realized in Canada wffiich is absolutely necessary for the efficient and efficacious solution of the grave domestic problems with which we are now face to face. And therefore in regard to the Locarno treaty, or in regard to other treaties or conventions which may be submitted to this parliament, I hope that we may reasonably anticipate that this House o!f Commons, laying aside all merely party prejudices, all merely personal ambitions, may act in a spirit of unity and with the supreme desire to maintain a solidarity of public opinion in Canada with respect to inter-imperial and international matters. In the exercise of that discretion may we not reasonably hope that those who succeed us in filling the highest offices in the gifts of the people of Canada shall only undertake such inter-imperial and international responsibilities as may be undertaken with the general approval of all sections of the country, and so insure that the action of parliament, and of the government which this parliament maintains and sustain^, shall have the approval not only of a majority of the electoral constituencies throughout Canada, but also have the substantial support and co-operation of the constituencies in every important section, district or province of the Dominion? I am confident, Mr. Speaker-and my sole excuse for speaking is that I feel so strongly about this matter-that it is only by restricting all our external commitments and obligations within such limits as to merit and obtain the general approval, as I said, of each and every section of Canada, that we can ever hope to have such cordial co-operation between the peoples who compose the Canadian electorate as will enable us to solve our domestic problems in such a manner and so successfully as to maintain the continued solidarity and unity of the great Canadian nation, and thereby promote for all time the peace, progress and prosperity of this country, in which we were born, in which we will die and which will be the home of our children and our children's children for all future time.

subtopic: PROCEDURE GOVERNING NEGOTIATION, SIGNATURE AND RATIFICATION
speechtext:
It is much to be deplored that a subject of this magnitude should be brought before parliament in the dying hours of the session. For many years, due I suppose to a desire to take a rest from the exciting conditions of the war, there seems to have been a disposition to avoid full and ample discussion of our outside affairs, whether they relate to interimperial relations or to external affairs generally. Perhaps that is due also to the fact that the people of Canada, their parliament and their government, have practically never exercised their full responsibility as a free nation in these matters, and have inherited from generation to generation the old colonial and childish attitude of relying upon somebody else to shape their foreign policy.
As regards this resolution, worded as it is, there ought to be no exception taken. It is, first, a ratification of the decisions taken unanimously by the last Imperial conference, as the proper policy and the proper procedure to be followed in order to establish interimperial relations upon a certain logical basis, -inasmuch as logic can apply to the extraordinary system of government under which we live.
But the latter part of the resolution is much more important. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Caban), in that magnificent oration to which I am sorry so few members listened, has suggested to the government that there is a discrepancy between the former part, dealing with the ratification of treaties and conventions affecting Canada, and the acceptance of any treaty, convention, or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, without reference to Canada. I do not know what was in the minds of the framers of this resolution; but, I take it to be this. The former part of this paragraph applies to treaties and conventions in which Canadian interests are specifically dealt with; and therefore such treaties and conventions ought to be governed by the procedure which we are called upon to ratify to-day. But, in addition, the government invites the co-operation of parliament and a declaration by parliament that no treaty, convention or agreement, whether Canada is mentioned or not, but involving military or economic sanctions, shall be accepted by the government of Canada without the approval of parliament. This is indeed much broader, and much more to the point. It means that the British government, answerable as it is to only one parliament in the empire, will be now warned in advance that it cannot count upon the support of Canada, in any
matter of external policy, unless the parliament of Canada has signified its acceptance and approval of such policy.
The first concrete application of this principle will undoubtedly be to the Locarno treaty. Unfortunately, Sir, we find ourselves in the strange position that we have not at hand the correspondence exchanged between the British government and the various dominion governments. The very spirit of this resolution has been violated in advance by withholding from the parliament of Canada and the other dominion parliaments all those exchanges of views which have passed between the British government and the various dominion governments with regard to the Locarno treaty. The Prime Minister has invited the attention of the House to and its approval of this resolution for two reasons. One object is that he, or any representative of Canada at the next Imperial conference, may be enabled to say that the parliament of Canada has approved what was done at the last conference, and the other to direct future policy. But, as regards the future, the government has no opinion to express. Are the representatives of Canada to go to London without any expression of opinion on the part of this parliament, on Locarno, for example? We are told that the situation here is the same as it is elsewhere. No, 6ir, Locarno has been discussed in almost every dominion parliament. In India, a resolution has been introduced, though disallowed by the government, to disapprove of Locarno. In Australia, the leader of the opposition, Mr. Charlton, has attacked' Locarno and the Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce, has not defended it. In Ireland, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Fitzgerald, and the leader of the opposition, Mr. Johnson, have made it quite clear that the Free State will not be bound by the treaty of Locarno and will not endorse it. In South Africa, Mr. Hertzog made it equally clear that he did not favour it, and when he challenged his opponent, General Smuts, to contradict him, Mr. Smuts stood up and practically endorsed the attitude of Mr. Hertzog. It is not going too far to say that the consensus of opinion, in all the parliaments of the empire, except the British parliament, has been against Locarno: not against what has been called the "spirit of Locarno," inasmuch as it means a move for peace, but as against the terms under which the "spirit" has expressed! itself in those various agreements, and more specifically against the undertaking by any of the free dominions of the empire to endorse the treaty and to assume its obligations. Now let us see what we have on hand.
International Agreements

It has been stated-the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) had it on his mind when he questioned the Prime Minister this afternoon-that the Locarno pact imposed no obligation, or would impose no obligation on the dominions, beyond what we have already assumed under the treaty of Versailles. Let us examine the documents as they stand. Take, first, the preamble of the main treaty, passing over the recitation of the powers of the plenipotentiaries. Germany, Belgium and France on the one hand, and Great Britain and Italy on the other hand agree to make a treaty. For what purpose? Let the treaty speak:
Anxious to satisfy the desire for security and protection which animates the peoples upon whom fell the scourge of the war of 1914-18;
Taking note of the abrogation of the treaties for the neutralization of Belgium, and conscious of the necessity of ensuring peace in the area which has so frequently been the scene of European conflicts;
Animated also with the sincere desire of giving to all the signatory Powers concerned supplementary guarantees within the framework of the Covenant of the League of Nations and the treaties in force between them; -
Have determined to conclude a treaty, etc.
Therefore, the very object of the treaty is to give "supplementary" guarantees. In the correspondence exchanged between the French and the English governments upon the proposal drafted by the Germans, Mr. Briand made this quite clear. Here is what he wrote to Mr. Chamberlain, through the French ambassador in London, on May 22, 1925:
By the words "within the framework of the Treaty of Versailles," the French government meant to specify that the pact proposed by Germany cannot in any way contradict, infringe or weaken the Treaty of Versailles, and represents an offer of complementary guarantees-
In other words, the treaty of Locarno means that over and above the "guarantees" given under the treaty of Versailles, the signatories to this new treaty are called upon to offer supplementary or complementary guarantees to Belgium and France-and to Germany, under certain conditions. With regard to Belgium, this is meant to replace the neutrality guaranteed to her by the treaties of 1831 and 1839, broken by the invasion of Germany in 1914, and abrogated since by the common consent of all parties to these treaties. With regard to France, those supplementary or complementary guarantees are to take the place of the treaties signed at Versailles, June 28, 1919, by the British and the American governments. Those two treaties have been thrown overboard, first, by the refusal of the American Senate to ratify the engagements taken by President Wilson; second, by the condition expressly stipulated by England,

that her engagements were subordinated to the ratification of the American treaty of guarantee.
As far as we are concerned was the idea ever entertained that we were a party to the treaty guaranteeing the neutrality of Belgium? Has it ever been contemplated that we should be a party to the treaty of 1919 regarding France? As regards the treaty guaranteeing the' neutrality of Belgium nobody would entertain that idea. As regards the treaty with France, Sir Robert Borden exacted and obtained a specific article which made the Dominions absolutely immune in that respect. Therefore if the Canadian government undertook at the next Imperial conference to recommend to this parliament adherence to the treaty of Locarno, that would mean that we would be assuming engagements, subject of course to ratification by the Canadian parliament, over and beyond what was contemplated by any preceding govern-hent; and very material additional obligations would be assumed by Canada as well as by any other dominion that would adhere to that treaty.
But it may be said, it has been said: Are we not already tied up by Article 10 of the Versailles treaty? We hear frequently of article 10, but I do not think many people have pondered over its terms. Let us read it now:
The members of the league undertake to respect and preserve, as against external aggression, the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all members of the League. In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression, the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
Later on, it is provided that such decision of the council must be unanimous. Moreover this very broad and vague obligation was discarded in practice, on the part of the dominions, first by the protest made by Sir Robert Borden immediately after he signed it, second by the protest made before the assembly of the League of Nations, by Mr. Doherty, representative of the late Conservative government, then by Sir Lomer Gouin, then by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe): and finally in Geneva a vote was passed upon and carried unanimously, but for the one opposing vote of Persia, which practically frees us from all responsibilities arising from article 10. How can it be said now that the application of article 10 of the treaty of Versailles entails any such obligation as can be compared with the very con-ciete obligation we would undertake if we adhered to the Locarno treaty?

International Agreements
But it is said further:" After all, this is a move for peace; should we not help morally and politically the British government in any move that they may make for peace?" Is it a move for peace? Has it been received by the thoughful opinion of Europe and America as an instrument of peace? Let us look into the matter for a moment. Supposing it does advance the cause of peace as between Germany on the one hand and France and Belgium on the other, this is a very 4 p.m. small and limited spot on the continent of Europe and the one where there is the least danger of a new war arising. It still leaves open the whole of the Balkan problem, the relations between Poland and Russia, the relations betwen the various European nations interested in the spoils of the old Turkish empire. The whole of the Near East question is left open. Therefore it cannot be defined as a move for the establishment of peace in Europe. But as far as is goes, does it make for peace between France and Germany? Let us look for a moment in the treaty itself. Article 1 reads:
The high contracting parties collectively and severally guarantee, in the manner provided in the following articles, the maintenance of the territorial status quo resulting from the frontiers between Germany and Belgium and between Germany and France and the inviolability of the said frontiers as fixed by or in pursuance of the Treaty of Peace signed at Versailles on the 28th June, 1919-
Nothing bad in that. But it goes on:-
-and also the observance of the stipulations of articles 42 and 43 of the said treaty concerning the demilitarized zone.
In other words one of the basic conditions of the treaty is that Germany will remain disarmed on the right bank of the Rhine, but that France will remain free to arm herself to the teeth up to the limit of her frontiers on the left bank of the Rhine. As long as those clauses exist in the treaty of Versailles there is no certainty of peace as between France and Germany, because it is essentially an unjust disposition which was adopted in the turmoil of passions still boiling after the war, but which every thoughtful person realizes is a false basis of peace. Article 2 specifically provides:
Germany and Belgium, and also Germany and France, mutually undertake that they will in no case attack or invade each other or resort to war against each other.
So far, so good; but immediately the article goes on to say that this stipulation, or in other words this mutual engagement not to resort to war or to attack or to invade each other, shall not apply in the following cases:
1.	The exercise of the right of legitimate defence, that is to say, resistance to a violation of the undertaking contained in the previous paragraph, or to a flagrant breach of articles 42 or 43 of the said treaty of Versailles, if such breach constitutes an unprovoked act of aggression and by reason of the assembly of armed forces in the demilitarized zone immediate action is necessary.
We shall see in a moment how this is to be interpreted in the light of the other conventions signed on the same date. Again the undertaking not to make war against each other does not apply in the case of:
2.	Action in pursuance of article 16 of the covenant of the League of Nations.
In other words, if France passes over the territory of Germany to enforce a decision of the council of the League of Nations, this is not an act of aggression on her part. But if Germany undertakes to protect her territory. against that invasion by a French army going for example to the rescue ot Poland, this is an act of aggression under the terms of article 16 of the treaty of Versailles Under that treaty, to invade your neighbour's territory under certain circumstances constitutes no aggression, but to defend your country against invasion constitutes aggression. That is the Versailles spirit. But the worst is contained in paragraph 3. Again the stipulation not to resort to war shall not apply in the ease of:
3.	Action as the result of a decision taken by the assembly or by the council of .the League of Nations or in pursuance of article 15, paragraph 7, of the covenant of the League of Nations, provided that in the last event the action is directed against a State which was the first to attack.
What is this? Paragraph 7 of article 15 is precisely that disposition of the treaty of Versailles under which Mr. Poincare, against the advice of the council of the League of Nations, against the advice of his allies, the British and the Italians, invaded the Ruhr in conjunction with the Belgian army and maintained occupation there with a negro army, for nearly a year-increasing by an immense amount the debt of Germany, without reducing by one iota the claims of France as against Germany, and bringing the whole of Europe again to the brink of war. Well, under this treaty, both France and Germany reserve to themselves the right to act exactly as Mr. Poincare did in the invasion of the Ruhr. Will anybody tell us that this is a sure guarantee for peace, and that if we adhere to it we are enabling the British government to establish peace between France and Germany?
Article 3 stipulates that:
In view of the undertakings entered into in article 2 of the present t-reaity, Germany and Belgium and Germany and France underbake to settle by peaceful means and in the manner laid down herein all questions of every kind-
International Agreements

-and so forth. This is the engagement to resort to arbitration, but always reserving to themselves the right to attack without resorting to arbitration in the cases that I have just mentioned.
But there is worse than that. If you go through those four arbitration treaties which follow-one between Germany and France, one between Germany and Belgium; one between Germany and Poland, and one between Germany and Czeoho-Slovakia -you will find that in the very first article it is said most positively that:
This provision-
-the undertaking to resort to arbitration,-*
-does not apply ito disputes arising out of events prior to the present convention and belonging -to the past.
Now I ask, viewing the surface of things as they have been and as they are still in Europe, what possible cause of conflict, what possible cause of bickering, can be imagined for the next twenty-five years to come between any of those nations, which a government desirous of making war could not tie up with some cause anterior to the signature of the treaty, whether it relates to frontiers, to economic sanctions, to rights of way-to any of those multitudinous questions which have been dealt with or mentioned in the treaty of Versailles? Those are precisely the causes that will keep Europe in a turmoil and in a state of unrest so long as the diplomats and1 the governments of Europe have not made up their minds to tear down that monument of folly and iniquity, the treaty of Versailles, and rebuild a real treaty of peace in Europe.
Now, under article 6 of the treaty of Locarno, it is stipulated that the whole of the Versailles treaty remains untouched. This in itself is an untruth. The treaty of Locarno is an amendment of the treaty of Versailles. Besides, anybody who has followed the trend of events for the last seven years, knows that in fact at least, if not in law, the treaty of Versailles has been amended or disregarded in many respects by every country in Europe. Therefore to profess that the object of the treaty of Locarno is to maintain the treaty of Versailles is at the outset to nullify the moral effect of the spirit of Locarno, and. secondly, to establish this so-called movement for peace on a basis of deceit-deceit against public opinion the world over, but especially against those unfortunate peoples in Europe who are in such sore need of real political direction towards peace. Need I say that

this declaration would mean, if we adhere to it, that we approve of all the dispositions of Versailles? That after seven years of experience, notwithstanding the happy moves made by Sir Robert Borden, by Sir Lomer Gouin, by Mr. Doherty and by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to disengage us from that clap-trap, we would again undertake, by the simple acceptance of this one short section of the treaty of Locarno, to revive the corpse of Versailles? It would mean that we approve of the regime of the French in the Saar, that we approve of the disposition relating to the future of Austria, of article 80 under which-violating the basic principles upon which the United States entered the war, violating the professions of faith uttered by Mr. Asquith and other British statesmen-we have forbidden a crushed nation, deprived of nine-tenths of its possessions, ever to decide its future according to its needs. It would mean we make ourselves the guarantors of the system established in Upper Silesia against all the principles of public policy, against the most-solemn promises of good faith that were given by the council of the League of Nations, that the status of those populations would be decided under the principle of self-determination. It would mean that we still maintain those provisions by which the German nation has been deprived of all her colonies, thereby making us a party to this absurd policy of saying: That whilst we, British, occupy one-fourth of the surface of the earth, that whilst France is in possession of one-half of the continent of Africa-France a nation with no surplus population-we keep as a basis of policy the inhibition to a great nation of eighty million people to find expansion for her population and for her merchandise. And you think peace can be established upon that basis? It would mean the maintenance of these absurd articles declaring that Germany is the sole responsible party for the war, that the former rulers of the German empire are culprits before public opinion and should be brought before the tribunals, not of disinterested nations, but before tribunals instituted by their victors. Now, Sir, it may be that in colonial and savage countries where what is now known about the war has not penetrated, this notion is still sincerely entertained; but there is not one right-thinking man in Europe today, whether he be French, English, German, Dutch or Italian, who still believes that. I have in my hand protests that are being signed by hundreds of the best-thinking men and women in England and France against those ridiculous articles; not through any

International Agreements
high sense of generosity, but because they realize, being on the spot, knowing the condition of affairs, that so long as such nonsense remain in a public document supposed to contain the wisdom of the diplomacy of the world, there can be no moral peace in Europe; and as long as there is no moral peace there will always be danger to material peace.
Fortunately, the British government realized that they should not commit the governments of the dominions, either directly or indirectly, to such a piece of doubtful policy, and they made the reservation which the Prime Minister read this afternoon. To show how little these matters are followed in this country, when the text of the Locarno treaty appeared, one of the best-informed newspapers of Canada usually, the Montreal Gazette, expressed great surprise at this "new departure", forgetting that the same principle had been laid down, in almost the same words, in the treaty of guarantee signed on June 28, 1919; that a few years later, when Mr. Lloyd George was endeavouring with Mr. Briand to reach some terms of agreement as between England and France and to substitute something else for the discarded treaty of guarantee, the same reservations were introduced into the draft treaty of Cannes of 1922. So in England, much more than in Canada, do they realize that it is not only proper, but that it has become a fixed principle of imperial policy, that the British government has not the right to commit the action of any of the free dominions associated with England without the full consent of the responsible governments and parliaments of those dominions. The only difference is that in the first instance, at the particular request of Sir Robert Borden, the action of parliament was reserved. I have not the text here, but it can easily be found. In article 5 of the treaty of guarantee, it is stated in exactly the same terms as in the treaty of Locarno that the present treaty shall impose no obligation upon any of the British dominions unless the "parliament" of such dominion signify its acceptance thereof. That is so under the treaty of 1919. Under the terms proposed by Mr. Lloyd George to Mr. Briand, there was a slight modification. I quote from memory, but I feel sure it is correct:
The present treaty shall impose no obligation uipon any of the dominions unless and until it is approved by the dominion concerned.
There was no mention of either parliament or government; but it was the same disposition, the same principle. In this later treaty, reference is made to "governments", no doubt, 14M1-303
as the Prime Minister stated this afternoon, because India was then added to the dominions, marking a new step in the emancipation of the various portions of the British Empire. But so far as Canada is concerned, and so far as all self-governing dominions are concerned, is it not quite proper and according to the spirit of our constitution and of the principles of British government, that this parliament should assert that it is supreme in such matters and that no government, whatever its majority or whatever the principles of its individual members, will have the right to commit Canada, not only by adhering to a written treaty, but by giving its moral adherence to an unwritten agreement which may carry military or economic sanctions?
Anyone familiar with the trend of diplomacy knows that the great art of diplomats, and not only the last but the most frequent resort of governments, is the undertaking of unwritten engagements. Public opinion is then prepared to accept them and finally, when everything is practically agreed upon, parliament is asked to ratify them. Therefore I think it was proper for the government to enlarge the scope of this motion and to invite an expression of opinion by parliament, not only upon Locarno, not only upon the ratification by parliament of any written agreement of which everyone knows, but also to declare that no government has the right to commit the action of the country, either economic or military, without previous approval by parliament.
It may be said that the days when the British government would think of including the dominions in the purview of its diplomatic action or political undertakings is long past. It is not so long past. In the correspondence exchanged between the British and Canadian governments, previous to the ratification of the Versailles treaty, I find over the signature of Lord Milner, then Secretary of State for the Colonies, the following words:
The king, by a single aot, wouttd bind the whole empire, as it is Tight that he should so [do], but that act would represent the considered judgment of his constitutional advisers in all self-governing states of the empire, because it would be merely giving effect to an international pact which they had all agreed to.
In other words, Lord Milner held that because we had been represented at Versailles -in what manner everyone knows or should know,-the simple fact that the treaty was
ratified by the king, or by the English representatives of the king, should bind all the dominions. Fortunately, the Prime Minister

All the sympathy of the English was on the side of Germany so long as Germany had not the pretensions of becoming in her turn a maritime and a colonial power. Friendly relations with England may last a long time or may be short. Revolution may produce certain issues. As far as I am concerned, none of the issues would frighten me. I would be just as much prepared for close partnership within the empire as for independence; of course I would rather have independence. From a Canadian point of view or from a British point of view, let us serve notice to the world at large, not in any spirit of animosity towards Great Britain, but in full consciousness of what we owe to our people, that Canada is prepared to uphold morally any .real move for peace which may be taken in Europe or anywhere, but that Canada is not prepared to arm her youth and to spend her millions for the sake of any foreign policy with which we are not connected by necessity and from which Canada is disconnected by all the exigencies of her natural situation. That is the policy that Sir John A. This fact is imposing itself upon us in spite of all our professions of imperialism. One thing which I have never been able to understand, from a British point of view, is how it is that so few Canadians of note have endeavoured to realize that the basis of our foreign policy is and must be the Monroe doctrine.
