Go to Belgium, go to Holland, go to Switzerland, to those small countries that, thank heaven, are not engaged in the turmoil of imperial policy which has been the curse of the world, but which nevertheless live in close contact with those ambitious and rapacious nations, have to understand foreign affairs-talk for example, to a dog-driver in the streets of any Belgian town, and he will speak to you of German policy, of French policy, of English policy, not of course with the same knowledge as Sir Edward Grey or Sir Austen Chamberlain possess, but with a degree of understanding which very few Canadian statesmen have

shown so far in regard to foreign affairs. Why? Because those problems are home problems to him, because the fate of his nation is at stake in the event of a quarrel between France and Germany.
Is it the case with us? For one century previous to the Great war England had many wars. Did we think we had to have one imperial policy at the time of the Crimean war? Fortunately we did not; we had sensible statesmen then who kept us out of the fray. Did we think we had to go to the rescue of England because she wanted to paint half the area of Africa red? Did we think we were bound to go and bombard Peking in order to compel the Chinese to absorb opium to enrich some poppy planters in India who wanted to make more money? That was one of those great "civilizing wars" which fortunately we did not have to share in. Did we have to share in about thirty wars that Great Britain has been engaged in since the downfall of Napoleon up to the last war, extending over just one century? Not in one of them except the South African war. There the one imperial policy began to make itself felt, there we began to be clap-trapped by the same kind of propaganda which caught us in the last war. But surely after that experience of the one imperial policy, is it not time that we come back upon our own soil and appeal to the conscience of our people and ask them to have one national policy? You can never have one national policy if at the same time you run such risks as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St George has so very delicately pointed to this afternoon.
But I repeat, Mr. Speaker, though perhaps it may hurt the feelings of some hon. members here, I think it is just as well to go to the root of the thing now, it is just as well to realize that if at any one of these future conferences such undertakings and engagements as were taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1897, in 1899 and in 1909 are still resorted to in vague terms, moral or verbal engagements will be forced upon us later by an appeal to us that they are engagements of honour and all that, then it will be too late to settle the issue and avoid the consequences. Although I may have a very different conception of empire from that* entertained by several hon. members, I do not think there is one here who has more love for this country than I have. Perhaps my heart is small, but when I think of the sacrifices that have been made by eight generations of my forefathers to make something of Canada, when I think of my seven children who will be Canadian citizens and will have to make such

So far as England and the empire go, I am not in a hurry to lose that connection. As I have often said before, I appreciate our connection with England; but our best manner of appreciation is to show the rulers, the business men and diplomats of England that we are just as intelligent as they are; that we realize our situation just as they realize theirs, that we have a duty to perform to Canada just as they have a duty to their own country. If imperial association can last and if an imperial policy can be fruitful of results, it will be through each portion of the empire thinking of itself first, not through any selfish spirit of absolute disinterest, but in order to start on a sound basis of internal and external policy and join hands with England every time her rulers make a move for real peace in the world, but also to resist any attempt to drag us once more in foreign wars. We should join hands, I repeat, every time England may associate with any group of nations in the interest of peace, when her own interest lies in peace; every time she makes for justice, because her interests lie in the preservation of justice; every time she prevents or endeavours to prevent any nation from dominating, because it is to her interest that no nation should
dominate. Then, I say as a Canadian and a British subject, I approve of that move, and I give it my moral support. There I say British, yes, but Canadian first; if necessary, secession from Britain rather than the sacrifice of Canada; Canada in partnership with Britain so long as it is possible, but Canada first and forever.

The purpose of this resolution is to approve the procedure proposed at the Imperial conference of 1923 for the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties affecting Canada, and, before the ratification of any treaty can be made, to require the formality of its approval by parliament. It may be in some ways a cumbersome procedure, but it is also a great and necessary safeguard. Legislation lias to be passed by parliament, but if it does not work properly, parliament may repeal it. Treaties, once entered into, cannot so easily be put aside; they may bind our successors in office and our country to momentous undertakings, and it is only reasonable that these undertakings be entered into after full discussion and under the sole responsibility of the representatives of the people.

The Locarno treaties, to be properly understood, must be studied in the light of the treaties and covenants which, since the war, have been proposed or passed [DOT] with a view to preventing future wars and securing a peaceful and amicable or judicial settlement of all difficulties which may arise between nations.
It is unnecessary to recall that the war, on the side of the allies, was fought as a war to finish wars, with the set purpose of creating after it conditions which would absolutely prevent the recurrence of such brutal, bloody and stupid conflicts, and the League of Nations was constituted mainly for that purpose. The covenant contains provisions whereby states are obliged to endeavour by peaceful methods to settle their differences, but it does not enforce an Obligatory peaceful settlement of a conflict. Later, the protocol for the pacific settlement of international disputes was submitted to the consideration of the different countries, members of the league. Under the covenant the decision to submit a dispute to arbitration or judical settlement was to be arrived at through an understanding between both litigants. The main purpose of the protocol was to provide that arbitration, or submission to judicial settlement, could be resorted to at the instance of one party alone. Arbitration of all international differences or their submission to the Permanent Court of International Justice was made compulsory; all wars of aggression were prohibited and all wars, resorted to in violation of the undertakings contained in the covenant or in the protocol, were branded as wars of aggression. The protocol was rejected by the British Empire; some other way to settle the situation had to be found and the Locarno agreements were negotiated and signed on the 16th of October, 1925. So far Germany had been left out of the League of Nations, and she was not invited to be a party to the Geneva protocol. The obligations imposed upon her by the treaty of Peace, though apparently voluntarily agreed to, had really been forced upon her, as she was not in a position to refuse to submit to them; these obligations were liable to be repudiated as contracted under duress.

That the present treaty shall impose no obligation upon any of the British dominions or upon India, unless the government of such dominion or of India signifies its acceptance thereof.
The question is now: Should Canada adhere to this treaty and submit herself to the obligations which it involves? But for the fact that Germany was not a party to it, the Geneva protocol was a much more effective weapon to promote international peace than the Locarno agreements. The purpose of the Geneva protocol was to make compulsory arbitration, or judicial settlement of international disputes, the law of the world, and if it had been adopted by the principal nations of Europe it might have been reasonably hoped that Germany and the other countries would ultimately have agreed to it. All wars under it could only take place in the name of the general international interest. The Locarno agreements are more local in character. They perpetuate the system of alliances of certain countries against others, and recourses to wars, for local and private reasons, under certain conditions are allowed to subsist. As the Geneva protocol was to apply to a greater number of countries, conflicts arising out of it might have been more frequent, but normally all the signatory countries would have united, in the name of law and order, against the infringer, and the application of economic sanctions should have been sufficient to bring a settlement. A conflict arising out of the Locarno treaty, being more local in character, might again create a situation which would strain all the resources of our country. Yet, Canada refused to adhere to the Geneva protocol because she did not want to accept its rigid provisions of economic and military sanctions in practically every future war. Surely there is no more reason why we should assume greater risks under the Locarno agreement.

At the time the treaty of Versailles was signed, treaties of guarantee were entered into between France and Great Britain, and France and the United States. These treaties were not ratified, but the treaty of guarantee by Great Britain in favour of France against German aggression contained a clause that it would not be binding upon the dominions or upon India unless ratified by the governments of the dominions or of India. The first thing to notice in respect of this treaty is that Great Britain and Italy are parties to it, not for the direct safeguarding of their respective frontiers or of their peculiar direct interests; they are parties to it only indirectly, as sureties, to guarantee that both Germany and France or Germany and Belgium will carry out the terms of the treaties of arbitration negotiated between them at Locarno. If Great Britain was to declare war under this treaty, it would be a war of police, resorted to in order to compel one country to abide by the terms of a convention with another. There is a vast difference between a war of that kind and a war of defence in which the life of the empire would be at stake. The duties which are imposed upon us by our association in the Britannic commonwealth cannot go so far as to involve us in a war of aggression or in a war of intervention between foreign nations.
The casus foederis may be controvertible; it may not be understood by nations living thousands of miles from the scene of the conflict as it would be by peoples living near it; it may give rise to different interpretations amongst our own population, and promote disunion and discord. It is not a case where we can bind ourselves so long in advance. We must let the parliament of the day decide the issue when it arises, and we woidd be failing in our duty towards future generations if we were to bind them, hand and foot, to all wars which may result from the engagements of Great Britain at Locarno.
To assume obligations which may lead to war, our country must have something at stake. This stake must be something which
directly affects us, and must be of sufficient importance to be commensurate with the risks which such an undertaking involves. We have a great interest in the maintenance of peace in Europe, but we have this interest in common with the other countries, and our responsibilities incurred to reach this aim should not be greater than those of the other countries. With that end in view we have assumed obligations under the covenant of the League of Nations, and we will fulfil them to the best of our ability, but our moral duties should not go further.
I am not a pessimist, and I have great hopes that the democracies will succeed in preventing a recurrence of the unfortunate events of the past decade, that common sense will prevail and find ways and means, other than war, to effect a peaceful settlement of the conflicts as they arise between states, that civilization has reached a stage where arbitration and judicial settlement will decide these issues; but we must all admit that, as a result of the war, the situation in Europe is not yet perfectly adjusted, that the peoples of Europe are not all yet reconciled to the alterations and modifications brought about by the war; that resentments, envy and fear still prevail, and that time alone can cure all that. I quite understand that Great Britain, being part of the European continent, should have felt bound to intervene in order to promote a readjustment along peaceful lines, but I fail to see how a country two thousand miles away can undertake to act forcibly as arbitrator between European states, or how she can feel any legal or moral obligation to intervene on one side or on the other in order to impose its solution on unwilling populations. To ratify such a treaty would be to assume a role which does not befit our country, and which is unnatural.
There is the solidarity of the empire to be considered, but it is, to my mind, a solidarity in defence; it is not one which can extend to wars of encroachments, or wars of police to restore peace between foreign countries, or to punish certain foreign countries for their misdeeds. Our country has the advantage of a geographical situation which reduces to a minimum the risks of encroachments on the part of its neighbours. She is from that standpoint in a most enviable position. On the other hand, climatic conditions and the configuration of her inhabited territory create difficulties which are not of easy solution; her transportation problems constitute a burden which is heavy to carry; she has immeasurable natural resources, but they are as yet mainly undeveloped. All her
International Agreements

energies are required if she wants to overcome these difficulties and secure her full development. Under these conditions, even looking at it from the standpoint of the interest of the empire as a whole, would it be wise for Canada to divert her energies from these problems, to sacrifice her own interests in order to assume heavy obligations for the purpose of contributing by force to the restoration of order on the European continent? I sincerely believe that our obligations to ourselves and our obligations to the empire may be fulfilled in a way to yield better profit, for all parties concerned, by limiting as much as possible our external undertakings and applying ourselves to the development of our country.
The constitutional development of Canada is based to a large extent on precedents, and since confederation our rights and our powers in matters of international intercourse have been increased and widened on the sole authority of precedents and common sense. Since the war it has been the practice for Canada to be represented at all international conferences where obligations were to be assumed in the name of the British Empire, and to be a party to the treaties which embodied the decisions of the conferences. Certain rules were laid down at the Imperial conference of 1923 to govern the procedure to be followed for the negotiation and signature of these treaties when they were to bind the empire as a whole. They provided that the full powers should be in the form employed at Paris and Washington. This rule was not adhered to at Lausanne and at Locarno and the dominions were left out of the negotiations. The dominions were not invited, their participation was not looked for and as there was no wish on the part of the other contracting parties to bind the dominions, these cannot be expected to involve themselves in military undertakings to enforce the provisions of the treaties mentioned. Our claims to an international status corresponding with the status which we occupy in the League of Nations have been constantly pressed since the Versailles treaty by all parties in Canada, and they are well known. To assume responsibilities under treaties contracted without our participation would be to impair or sacrifice this status. It is true the Locarno treaty provides that the dominions shall be bound by this treaty only if they ratify it, but to adhere to it would be to sanction a practice which is not in harmony with our present status.
Some will say that to refuse to ratify such a treaty would be to impair the diplomatic unity

of the empire. But we are an autonomous country, with the right to govern ourselves as we see fit. Has the foreign policy of Great Britain since the war or before, always been such as to warrant our unequivocal en-dorsation? At the khaki election of 1918 the policy of the British government was to maintain firmly the entente with France, to make Germany pay, if necessary by searching their pockets, and to bring to trial and punish the kaiser and the other war criminals. A little later, without change of government, there was a complete reversal of British policy. Germany was encouraged not to fulfil her engagements, she was induced to resist the attempts of France to extract partial reparation, and the whole British policy became permeated to saturation with a franco-phobia which delayed the restoration of normal conditions and increased the dissatisfaction and the resentments which already existed. That policy was a failure and there was another reversal of policy. All these policies were determined without our participation, without our consultation. They never represented the concerted opinion of the governments of the autonomous dominions. Diplomatic unity, without consultation and without co-operation, means diplomatic servility, and as presently constituted it cannot be acknowledged as a factor in the shaping of the policies of Canada.
There is no doubt that when Great Britain is at war the dominions are also at war, but they are merely in a state of passive belligerency; active belligerency or actual participation in the war does not necessarily follow; it is a matter which is left at the discretion of their respective governments. In this case, the ratification of the treaty of Locarno means necessarily active belligerency, whilst nonratification means only passive belligerency. It is not for us to bind ourselves and to bind our children to active belligerency in a future war between France and Germany arising out of this treaty. We have no direct interest in such a war. Our association in the Britannic commonwealth is not such as to involve the taking of such risks in order to increase the importance, the power, the strength and the prestige of the political leaders of one of the associated nations of this commonwealth, or to enforce policies decided and determined without our participation. We have no business to interfere, in the name of law, order or civilization, in conflicts which may arise under this treaty, as we hold no mandate for that purpose.

International Agreements
There is therefore, in my humble opinion, no reason whatever why we should ratify the treaty entered into by Great Britain at Locarno, and in the best interest of our country parliament should refuse to adhere to it. To vest in the government of Great Britain or in the government of Canada the right to embroil our country in adventures of that nature without the participation of parliament, would be a policy pregnant with the most dire results, and undermining the whole democratic structure of our country.

I represent a soldier and British-born constituency. This is the fourth time the present matter has come before the House this session and very little has been said with respect to it by hon. gentlemen on this side. Sir John A. Macdonald was satisfied with the status of this country. He did not ask the British government to increase the status of Canada. Five hundred thousand soldiers who went to the front and fought for civilization in France and Flanders were satisfied with Canada's status. Fifty thousand of those gallant men lie buried in those countries; they were content to fight even unto death under Canada's status. They fought for Canada's status but did not ask that any change should be made in it; they did not ask for any increased status for Canada. Such being the case I think the civilians who stayed at home should also be satisfied with the status of this Dominion.
Of the links that used to bind Canada to the Motherland what links remain to-day? First there is our allegiance to the British crown; secondly there is the right of appeal to the Privy Council; thirdly any treaties into which we enter must have the sanction of the mother of parliaments. We are not an independent nation, or a nation at all; we are a link in a chain of free commonwealths within and making up the British Empire. We never were a nation. Talk about annexation with the United States! There is no feeling at all in Canada in favour of it, nor for independence either. Talk about Canada being independent, a country of nine million souls, competing with or withstanding a nation of 110,000,000 people! Why if we were independent a foreign fleet might sail up the St. Lawrence and we would not have as much as a rowboat to oppose it with because our toy navy is locked up in a garage at Halifax.
I invite consideration of the question of what our duty is as a member of the empire. We are shortly to have an Imperial conference. Where is the agenda; what will Canada bring up, and what is the government's policy? The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to sit down at such a conference with the representatives of the sister dominions, Australia, New Zealand and others, with the object of seeing what could be done to better the conditions of the component parts of the empire and foster inter-imperial trade and relations. The time has come for Canada to stop whining about our status, to stop complaining, to stop shouting from the housetops about our lack of status, which is a mere technicality, a mere academic question. The time has come for Canada to keep step with Australia and New Zealand; to sit in at a table with these sister dominions and discuss in a friendly, amicable and peaceful manner, in the interest of the good of the empire, the inter-imperial trade and economic problems and other inter-imperial problems and questions in a big, brotherly, united way; to consider our relations with the Motherland and try to assist the Mother Country to solve her economic problems and get some imperial results instead of attending these colonial conferences and adopting benevolent aloofness policies and whining and complaining about our status.
I am opposed to this resolution and intend to vote against it. My reason for that is that the whole resolution is based on the doctrine and principles of separatism. That is what it is, and nothing else. There was a colonial conference in 1922 or 1923, and what position did Canada take over there? The representatives of this country sat back and said: We are satisfied; we will not help; we will pursue a policy of drift and benevolent aloofness. Australia and New Zealand had a policy but we did not have any at all. We were satisfied to hold aloof and whine, like Ireland and South Africa, instead of being satisfied with the Motherland and with the happy conditions in which she has placed us and appreciate the debt of gratitude we owe her for maritime freedom. We should have unity of policy within the empire. We should be in law and fact, all parts of the empire, an international unit working all in unison and complete accord for the good of the empire and each and every part thereof. Instead of Canada's present position of shirking all empire responsibility, Australia's vigorous participation prejudices Canada in England, and Canada's aloofness hurts our country. We who in the darkest hours of the war were prepared to accept the protection of the British fleet and all the privileges we enjoy
International A greements

as part of the British Empire should now be prepared to accept some of the responsibility which that incurs; yet, on the other hand, we give nothing in return, except that we whine and complain about our status within the empire.
The status idea of Sir John A. Macdonald and other great statesmen of Canada was expressed in the statement, "A British subject I was born; a British subject I will die." Sir John was satisfied with the status of the country within the empire and made no demand for a change. We have been in session six months and a resolution is now presented to the House in its dying hours, when there is no adequate opportunity to discuss it. It is all very well for the hon. member for Labelle, to give his views on the subject. This is the fourth occasion on which he has spoken for two hours and a half on the same subject of Canada's status and independence. If Canada is to be talked out of the British Empire the hon. member for Labelle would have accomplished that many years ago. But Canada is not going to be either talked1 or written out of the British Empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British Empire. There is no demand for any change in the status of Canada to-day, so far as the city I represent is concerned. Before the session closes I hope the Prime Minister will lay on the table the agenda of the coming conference and let this House instruct him on the country's policy. I hope he will not follow in the footsteps of Ireland and South Africa, but will adopt the policy of Australia and New Zealand and try to help solve with all Canada's power the inter-imperial and difficult economic problems which confront the empire to-day. If an united effort is made, great benefit will accrue in the extension of the empire through all its parts. As Mussolini said the other day, "You who live in an empire have a sacred trust to perform." What he said of Italy is true of our great British Empire. He said, "A country does not belong to the people who live in it to-day. It is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present, and a trust for the future." Canada's status was good enough for Sir John A. Macdonald and his successors and the soldiers who fought in the South African and the late Great war. The war did not change Canada's status. I am utterly opposed to any change in Canada's status. I am opposed to separatism autonomy and further changing of our status. We are proud that Canada is an integral part of the greatest empire the world has even known. The war left us our status as it was. What Canada has

done the past thirty-five years she has done of her own volition, and voluntarily, and she would do the same thing over again, namely, come to the Mother Country's aid in her hour of peril. So the people of this country are satisfied with our present status.
Speaking of treaties, Canada sent gentlemen down to Washington in 1911 and made a treaty with reference to reciprocity. You all know what happened to them and their government. Where do we stand with regard to the Chicago diversion of waters? Not one line has been written to the British government regarding that particular matter, owing to our desire to deal with Washington ourselves. I asked a question of the government in regard to water diversion, and I received the answer that there had been no correspondence whatever with reference to that particular matter directly with the British government. We have allowed this question of diversion of water at Chicago to remain in abeyance, and where has it landed us? Nowhere, because of our failure to place our case with the British government.
Regarding the other treaties that have been made by Canada, where are we? The French, Australian, Belgian, West Indies-all failures. Speaking of the position of this country, I say that I do not believe in separatism. If we were to accept the Independent separatist views of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) the quicker Canada gets out of the British Empire the better for the rest of the empire. There are some 'links which bind Canada inseparably to the Motherland. But there are people who would abolish appeals to the Privy Council, who would alter the British North America Act, who would abolish the office of Governor General and of Lieutenant Governor, and who would have an Ambassador at Washington-an ambassador who would have no functions but be a figure head. Two ambassadors went down there in 1911 and almost landed Canada in economic annexation through reciprocity with the United States. When Canada sends delegates to the Imperial conference the House of Commons should instruct those delegates to eliminate the spirit of separatism entirely and instruct them to co-operate and not hold aloof. I hope the Prime Minister will lay on the table of the House the agenda for the coming conference and the policy of the government. The Premiers of Australia and New Zealand have already taken their parliaments into their confidence, and I see no reason why the head of this government should not follow suit and lay down a solid British Imperial policy, and a forward one.

International Agreements
I would urge a closer policy of trade union between the Mother Country and the various dominions; that they should sit round a table and try to solve our problems, instead of adopting a spirit of aloofness. Premier Ferguson in a speech dealt with the subject, and was in favour of closer trade union within the empire. The people of New Zealand and Australia are in favour of it, and I think we should favour it also. We are accepting all the privileges of citizenship within the empire, and should not be afraid to shoulder some of the burdens. By adopting this motion we are declaring for separatism all along the line. I am opposed to the doctrine set out in the motion, and the people of Canada are I believe also opposed to it. If this proposition had been placed by the government before the country the last general election, I believe we would have a membership of a different complexion. The time has come to stop whining and complaining. The facts should be placed before the country. I represent a city which has British ideals which favours British institutions and is entirely British imperial.
I am opposed to the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington. I believe it will cause Canada a good deal of trouble and do a lot of harm to our empire at Washington, as it did in 19(11, and I have no use for it. If the British authorities recommend the Locarno treaty as necessary for the defence of the empire, I think Canada should sign it. If Britain tells us our safety depends upon it, that settles it; let us adopt it unanimously. After accepting the rights, privileges and prerogatives of British protection, Canada should be prepared to accept some of the responsibilities and burdens. We should show our self-respect in that way and no longer permit the British taxpayer to provide for our Maritime protection. Instead of Canada taking the same position identically as South Africa and Ireland did as to their status within the empire, we should take our cue from New Zealand and Australia and be satisfied with our present status within the empire. What is that status? It is a status which was good enough for Sir John A. Macdonald, for the soldiers who fought the battles of the empire in the South African war and in the last war.
Why is this change proposed? There has been no demand so far as I can see for a change. This appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington is in my opinion another foolish example of the separatist idea. How long this will continue in Canada I
do not know; but I believe if a vote of the people was taken as to the status of this country within the empire, they would be satisfied with the present status of allegiance to the British crown, of appeals to the Privy Council, of ambassadors and in regard to many other matters that occurred during and after the war; they would side with our dear sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand. The policy of 1914 that parliament should be summoned and asked to sanction a matter of war is the right policy, but in minor matters and all other matters the government must take the responsibility as long as they are the government.
As regards sitting round the table with the sister dominions on constitutional and economical questions, I believe the government of the day should assume the responsibility, and on the government of the day so far as they are the government is the responsibility of seeing that when they go to the colonial conference they will represent the views of the people of Canada impartially and not hold aloof as they did at the last conference.
There is no demand for this resolution; in my opinion it is only an academic one and one which will not do any good. If these are the views expressed by the government in the House of Commons, and the Prime Minister and his government are for separatism and benevolent aloofness, it would be far better if Canada had no delegate at the coming conference and sent no one to wrongly express Canada's views. If we were to take the same position which New Zealand and Australia took at the last Imperial conference that would be the right view.
If the Canadian parliament will not say what are our rights in regard to constitutional matters, and stand by the empire and oversea dominions, I see no necessity for sending a delegate to the colonial conference. If the views of the hon. member for Labelle are the views of the people of this country, the quicker Canada gets out of the British Empire the better.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock one of the hon. members from Toronto (Mr. Church) had just taken his seat. It has not been my practice in this House to attack any hon. gentleman because of his personality, and
International Agreements

I do not propose to do so on this occasion. I wish however, to refer to some of the remarks of the hon. member, because I really do not think that the dignity of this House in debate, nor the serious and due consideration we should give to questions as important as this, is going to be helped by references to " the 50.000 soldiers that died overseas not being in favour of this form of resolution." The hon. gentleman makes many general allegations without substantiating them by one tittle of evidence. He charged the Prime Minister with having introduced this resolution as a separatist, as a man who is anxious for the separation of Canada from the Mother Country. Pie charged others who supported the Prime Minister from these benches, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), as 'being secessionists or separatists. I wish to dissociate myself from such statements especially as in this particular instance they were utterly unsupported.
The same hon. gentleman says: We are not a nation. Why are we not? We are a nation in the eyes of all those who signed the treaty of Versailles. We are a nation to the full extent that we desire to assert our nationhood. That is all that remains. He says he has had no chance to discuss this important question because it was introduced in the dying days of the session. I wonder how long the hon. gentleman would like to discuss the question, all the evening? He had all the evening if he wanted to take it. He could have had all to-morrow too if he wanted to debate it at still greater length. I wonder how long the hon. gentleman requires to discuss a question of this kind.
Then he said in closing that the colonial status was good enough for Sir John A. Macdonald, therefore it was good enough for him. I disagree with the hon. member's statement in the first place because I do not think Sir John A. Macdonald ever was satisfied with the colonial status. Many of his speeches in Hansard and many of his addresses in the country would indicate the contrary to be the fact. But even supposing Sir John A. Macdonald did believe in t'he colonial status, and so stated, I should like to ask the hon. gentleman: would he'be satisfied to be back in the same position as Sir John A. Macdonald was; would be be satisfied to do without the great inventions of modern science, to do exactly as they did in those pioneering days in Canada? Or would he prefer the present time with its involved nationhood and stand up with his fellow^Canadians to urge forward the status of this country until we achieve that independence within the 
commonwealth which all true Canadians desire?
In opening up the material portion of this discussion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on introducing the resolution. I do not think it is fraught with any great terrors either for this country or for Great Britain or for any other country. It is a very moderate resolution indeed. But I congratulate him because in introducing it, and indeed I hope subsequently when the House shall have endorsed it, he will have succeeded in consolidating the position to which we have attained by recognition, if not by actual declaration. I have in my hand an article which appeared in the Fortnightly Review of March, 1925, written by a famous English publicist, who signs himself Augur. It reads as follows:
In 1914 Great Britain went to war with Germany without consulting the view of the dominions. The dominions were not consulted before the war began, neither was their approval of the declaration of war asked for afterwards officially. But now the situation has undergone a complete change. The great dominions by their effort in the war, and with our consent, have acquired national status, not only within the empire itself but also among the states of the world. The confirmation of this is in the fact that the selfgoverning dominions of the empire have been admitted, with our approval, to full individual membership of the League of Nations. Thus, for better or for worse, the constitution of the empire has changed.
I refer these statements by an Englishmen, to the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church).
But it is yet in the making. The principle of consultation has been imposed, but the method of its practical application has not been discovered yet. The situation needs careful and delicate handling. The time is not ripe when wo can go into imperial consultation with a complicated, far-reaching problem. For a long time we shall be obliged to restrict ourselves to elementary, straightforward issues.
Even of it were fair, we could not consult the empire about a French or a Belgium interest. With the best will in the world the dominions would not be able to understand us, and certainly would refuse to follow us in assuming a binding obligation towards peoples which do not belong to the British commonwealth of nations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is an entrancing study to follow the slow evolution of a nation from almost a primary condition. I have done it in a meagre way. I should like to have had time and opportunity in my early years to have studied it thoroughly. When we study the political evolution of Canada we find it has passed from the day of fiscal domination to the day of fiscal freedom-that is, as free of fiscal domination as my hon. friends to the right will permit us to be; we have passed from economic enslavement to economic freedom; we have passed from a war slavery, or

International Agreements
almost that, to a war freedom. In the last instance it has been of recent consummation. It is interesting to know that Sir Robert Borden, the great leader of the Conservative party who preceded my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), insisted that there be inserted in one of the treaties which he assisted in drawing up, the tripartite treaty of 1919, a clause providing that none of the dominions should be bound unless its parliament consented thereto. - That was the first really definite break in our war unity. It is interesting in passing to note that by article 40 of the constitution of the Irish Free State agreed to by the British government, and of course by the Irish Free State, it is provided as follows:
Save in the case of acutal invasion, the Irish Free State shall not be committed to active participation in any war without the consent of the Dail Eirrean.
That is the Irish parliament. So I say the war unity of the empire itself has gone. Diplomatic unity is going.
Let not hon. members, Mr. Speaker, be disturbed at this steady evolution of a child into manhood. It is really not a disturbing thing, because after we have reached that condition where we are assuming our own responsibilities and undertaking all that is implied in our complete nationhood, we still are bound more firmly, more definitely and more completely to the Mother Country by ties of honour, of justice, of loyalty and of love, than any tie of a colonial or subject condition can ever bind us. I say it with all the strength I have, that I am satisfied Canada will remain more definitely a friendly part of the British commonwealth of nations as an independent nation within that commonwealth than she ever will as a state under conditions which compel her inevitable participation in all those complications in which England herself may be involved.
Let us advance another step. During the discussion this afternoon the Locarno treaty was mentioned, and that is the second point upon which I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister; we are now to have an opportunity through this resolution of discussing that treaty. I am sorry, however, that in his remarks he did not pronounce more definitely his own opinion or that of his government upon this matter. It is true that he intimated that with what he at present understood of the treaty he did not think he would be willing to commit himself to sign it but that he preferred to leave any definite statement until after the Imperial .conference in October.

If I were to attempt to analyze that answer I would first, in fairness to myself, require to study the correspondence in connection with that request; there may be a good deal more behind it than at .present appears. Nevertheless other so-called colonies, or others of our self-governing dominions, have come out as definitely in respect of this treaty as it is possible for governments to do. Hertzog in South Africa, for example, is in no uncertain position in that regard. I would like then, to ask a question and to endeavour in my feeble way to answer it: Why do some of the imperial authorities appear to be so extremely anxious for Canada and her sister dominions to tie themselves to this treaty?
In order to answer that question thoroughly it will be necessary to examine the treaty itself and its antecedents. In so doing I would. like the House to recall the struggle which took place in 1919 between Clemenceau and Wilson and Lloyd George. At that time Clemenceau, answering the dire fears of the French populace, had determined to insist not only upon a treaty of guarantee of assistance by England and1 the United States, but also to insist on the occupation of the left bank of the Rhine. Wilson and Lloyd George were not at all agreeable to this proposal and Tardieu, Clemenceau's right hand man and one of the most brilliant young men in France at that time, who has since written a very excellent story of the whole transaction, has this to say about the situation:
It was on Maroh 14, 1910, that Mr. Lloyd George and President Wilson proposed to M. Clemenceau, in place of the inter-allied occupation of an independent Rhineland, the undertaking by Great Britain and the United States to come immediately to the assistance of France in case the latter should be the object of an unprovoked aggression by Germany.
This proposal if accepted by England, would have been an unprecedented thing. Tardieu himself acknowledges this fact in his book:
I have said "unprecedented"; on that I would lay stress. England in the course of her history has entered into specific and temporary agreements with various continental countries but has never subscribed to any general and permanent obligation. She has at times lent her aid; she has never bound herseLf in advance to give it.
Yet we are asked in this instance to bind ourselves in advance. It so happened at that time that Lloyd George and Wilson did not agree with Clemenceau's views. Further meet-

International Agreements

ings were held, and at page 178 Tardieu describes what took place:
Mr. Olemenccau's mind is made up on the evening of the sixteenth and his decision expressed dn a note handed to the heads of the allied governments on the morning of the seventeenth. A proposal is made to js, which substitutes one guarantee for another. We refuse this substitution. We gratefully note, with the fullest appreciation of its value, the pledge offered and desire to accept it but only on the express condition that it be supplemented by most of the other guarantees demanded by us	
Clemenceau at that time exerted a most extraordinary pressure upon those with whom he was associated, and so successful was he chat on the 22nd of the month Lloyd George capitulated; Wilson had done so a few days previously. Tardieu records the incident at page 186 as follows:
Mr. Clemenceau holds his ground unmoved. We send note upon note (March 19, 20, 22, 28 and 31, and April 4, 5, 15, 16 and 19). We shoiw that no matter how important the results attained it remains indispensable to give the treaty a guarantee of execution, to give to France a material safeguard against a Germany which because o-f the war will have millions of trained soldiers for years to come. We show that occupation alone meets this double need. Day6 pass.
At last Mr. Clemenceau's indomitable will wins its end. Light begins to break. Slowly, prudently and patiently, he widens the opening and on April 20 at six oclock in the evening he secures-first of all- from President Wilson his approval of the provisions of chapter 14. On the morning of April 22. Mr. Lloyd George gives his approval also, but not without agan renewing his objections. Mr. Clemenceau, who for two days has been in agreement worth President Willson, maintains all has points-duration of the occupation, its possible extension; participation by the Allies. Mr. Lloyd George ends the discussion:
"Very well, I accept."
What had he accepted? Mr. Lloyd George on behalf of England and Mr. Wilson on behalf of the United States had agreed not only to give assistance to France in the event of an aggression by Germany, but had in addition assented to the inter-allied occupation of the Rhineland. That occupation was condemned by the radical elements in all countries; it was laughed at and ridiculed by the moderates everywhere, who looked upon it as a hopeless and stupid piece of Prussianism on the part of the allies. However, Lloyd George and Wilson committed themselves to it. They were to occupy the territory west of Essen and Cologne for five years; the territory immediately south of that, the central zone, for ten years and the territory still further south, close to the Saar basin, for fifteen years. In the event of Germany's failure to live up to the complete terms of the treaty-since moderated, as hon. gentlemen know-the interallied occupation of the Rhineland could have continued indefinitely. So we had this extraordinary situation arise.

Then, Mr. Speaker, the inter-allied occupation of the Rhine commenced; the terms of that occupation were so involved and so far-reaching that a very definite occurrence took place at a meeting of the war cabinet held later. But before coming to that I would like hon. members to realize exactly to what we have been committed in this particular treaty. The question of the future status of Canada in the British Empire .is one of extreme importance and one that I think demands the earnest consideration of this House. The British Empire is a new experiment in the world's history. Perhaps this is not the proper time to discuss some of the negotiations which took place before the Great war broke out. Half a dozen men, perhaps, have the decision as between peace and war, yet the great majority of the people who must suffer have nothing whatever to do with those causes responsible for war. Military people say that the way to prevent war is to be always ready for war, and I have a great deal of sympathy with their viewpoint; it seems natural that the proper way to preserve peace is to get ready for war, but what has been the experience of the past? You will find everywhere in history that when nations prepared for war they were immediately at war; the one inevitably followed the other. So if the nations go on arming and preparing for war we will have another war. The only way to get peace is to prepare for peace in the same way.

Just a word in regard to the consolidation of our empire. Some people ask how Canada is to protect herself in time of war, and where she would be if it were not for the protection of the British army and navy; sometimes we are called selfish and narrow because we are not prepared to maintain a large standing army and navy to protect our chores. Perhaps a good deal could be said along this line in regard to a navy; I do not know that 1 would' complain if we were just a little better equipped in that regard than at present. At the same time, however, where is the danger coming from? I was bom in the Old Country and perhaps my heart beats as warmly for Old England as any in this House, but I think the only danger likely to come to Canada will come from our connection with the imperial parliament. Switzerland lies in the centre of Europe, but die seems to be quite safe; Canada would also be safe so long as she did not become embroiled in the European squabbles which are so frequent. If we keep out of those troubles and attend to our own business we will have no war, unless it should be through the call of blood to help our Mother Country in distress.
I might say a few words in regard to the actions which took place in the Dominion parliament" in regard to treaty-making, but that matter was so well discussed this afternoon that I do not think it necessary to take up any more time. I hope some way may be found whereby the free nations of the British Empire may find some tie which will bind them together, but I agree with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) that if you bind that tie too closely and make it a fixed thing you will be taking the best means to destroy the unity of the British Empire. I believe in the strong bonds of affection and love which bind us to the Motherland; Canada should go on her way step by step, perhaps drawing near the time when she shall be a free nation entirely independent, and capable of directing both her internal and external affairs.
I believe great things are in store for this country of ours; I believe Canada has something to give the nations of the world that will work to the betterment of all mankind, and I for one look into the distant future for the day when Canada will become one of the great nations of the earth, making for the peace and welfare of not only her own people but of the rest of the world as well.

bridge, though, to be built shortly, not very far away from that bridge?
No. There is the Canadian Pacific railway bridge at Lachine, about ten miles away from the present Victoria bridge.
About seven I have been told. Is that to be a traffic bridge?
No, a railway bridge only.
Would it not have been better to provide for road traffic as well there? That would greatly relieve the Victoria bridge.
It would have cost a large sum of money to change the bridge.
Nothing like $15,000,000.

Besides, that bridge is
several miles from Victoria bridge and there is no connection between the two shores of the St. Lawrence where the heavy traffic is.

We heard a great deal
about that bridge in 1013 during a certain by-election.

As to the mixing of grain, last year the Turgeon commission, which investigated the grain trade very thoroughly, visited the harbour of Montreal, and I do not think they found there anything of the kind which has been mentioned by the hon. member for South Winnipeg.

I would advise the minister to make inquiry of the Trade and Commerce department. With respect to the increased earning power of the harbour board of Montreal, I find in the annual report of the harbour board for 1925 there is shown an increase of income and revenue account of $4,749,100, an increase of $366,985.44 over the previous year, due mainly to the increased income from the grain elevator system. The main increase comes from the grain trade, largely originated in western Canada. From that point of view alone do I take an interest in the matter. The report shows that the interest charges, which amounted to $1,161,000, showed an increase last year of $113,000. Now then, you are going to add another $350,000 to those interest charges if you put through this loan, and the harbour 
board will not be able to maintain payment of their interest charges. It will be impossible for them to do it, no matter how anxious they are.
Mr.,CAHAN:	As I have already said, I
do not intend to enter upon a discussion of the bridge. There may be differences of opinion as to whether or not the bridge should have been constructed under the supervision of the harbour commission, but this bill deals with an appropriation for the purpose of increasing the capacity of the harbour for the handling of grain, and1 that is a national undertaking. The hon. gentleman suggests that a great deal of American grain goes through the port of Montreal but the fact is, Sir, that every ton of American grain going through the port of Montreal brings down the unit cost of handling that grain, whether it be Canadian or American. It is a great advantage to the port that its elevators should be used to their full capacity and that we should have new elevators with a greater capacity, because the larger volume of grain going through Montreal-the mass trans-shipment, as it were -enables the harbour commission to transfer that grain at a less unit cost than would otherwise be the case. On that account I think these appropriations which are to increase the capacity of the harbour for handling grain will not only yield an income sufficiently large to pay interest and provide something in the way of sinking fund on the appropriation we are now making, but will, if the harbour board is managed as well and as economically in the future as it has been managed in the past, enable it to cut down the unit cost of handling Canadian grain. Therefore I think this appropriation is entirely justified, and I think it should be passed because it is a great national undertaking and in the interests of the whole country. But it seems quite unnecessary to enter upon a discussion of the bridge at this late hour; it was authorized by parliament over a year ago and has nothing whatever to do with this appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not wish to delay the
passing of this bill but I would not like to let the statement just made by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) in regard to the mixing of grain at Montreal go unchallenged. I am not going to be drawn into a discussion of the bridge, which as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) just said was provided for two years ago and which has nothing whatever to do with the subject under consideration. I have nothing to say in regard to the bridge, except

Montreal Harbour Commission
that I am rather surprised to hear my hon. friend oppose the construction of another bridge. Rightly or wrongly he received credit for winning a by-election in 1913 on the promise to build a bridge across the St. Lawrence, and we have had many bad half hours when people have urged us to carry out the promise made by the Hon. Mr. Rogers in 1913.
Is it the same Mr. Rogers?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the same genial Mr. Rogers. The mixing of grain is an old story; we heard it first with regard to Canadian grain being mixed in New York, Baltimore, Newport News and other ports. It is a fight between Canadian and United States transportation lines to get the business, and I know an effort has been made to say that grain was not going through the port of Montreal correctly. That statement was made to offset the proof brought home by us that there was mixing of grain in the elevators at Baltimore. As has already been stated, the Turgeon commission investigated that matter and found the report ili-founded, and I submit that it is not in the interests of Canadian transportation lines or Canadian trade for a member of this parliament to advertise that there is mixing of grain in Montreal, when it has been established by a royal commission that there is no such mixing.

The mixing has probably
been carried on since that commission was appointed; it is of a very recent date, and my hon. friend will find the certificate in his own office.

Only a few weeks ago, when we were visiting the harbour of Montreal, we called the attention of the harbour commissioners to an allegation which had been made to the effect that mixing was carried on in the elevators. The harbour commissioners, in the presence of myself and other hon. members of this House, gave a complete denial to that statement and pledged their honour that there was nothing like that done in the elevators of Montreal. If it is done it is contrary to law; it is a breach of faith between these commisioners and parliament and the country, and before any hon. gentleman undertakes to spread that allegation throughout the country he should produce the facts and make a charge, in order that a thorough investigation may be made. We all know that the royal commission which investigated that subject two years ago found the harbour commission absolutely clean in that respect.

I would like to
ask the minister if he would be good enough to furnish the information I requested previously in regard to the salaries of the officials of the harbour boards of Montreal and Quebec, other than the commissioners.

Unfortunately I have not
the list for Quebec; I have asked for it and expect to.receive it shortly. I have the list for Montreal, however, and I wil give it now:

Is there any difficulty
in getting the details concerning the Quebec harbour commission officials?
No.

There is no difficulty in
getting this information, but I have to aslj the harbour commission to supply it.

When will the ministei
give the committee these details?

II think I will be in a
position to give them in a day or two; I will undertake to give them within that time.

Will the minister have
the information on Wednesday?
Yes, I will have it on Wednesday.

It seems to me this is a sink-hole for Canada's millions; we now grant $12,000,000 more to a harbour commission which already owes $44,000,000. I had the opportunity once of travelling around the harbour with some other hon. members; we passed through a huge cold storage plant which had only one comer occupied-the rest all empty. If we lend millions to the harbour commission in Montreal, what will be left for western Canada with which to develop a harbour in Hudson bay? The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) made a vicious attack on the $3,000,000 in the estimates for the Hudson Bay railway, but I notice now that he is in favour of this item

Montreal Harbour Commission
of $12,000,000. In the Public Works estimates only $21,000 was provided for the province of Manitoba. They take millions from the federal treasury and lend it without any provision being made for reserve or sinking fund. I think that is unfair to Canada. Canada has wonderful resources, and I could hardly understand how those resources could be devoured, but I am finding out where they are going and how they are being used up. I think this legislation is absolutely unfair.

A few minutes ago the minister gave us the income of the Montreal harbour commissioners for 1921 and 1925. Will he give us the tonnage for the same years in order that we may determine how the tonnage is growing in comparison with the income?

May I quote an extract from the Turgeon Grain Commission, which is considered the most authentic authority on the grain trade that Canada has ever had? This is supplementing what has been said by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and by the Minister of Finance:
No complaints are made touching grain shipped through Canadian channels and out of Canadian ports.
My hon. friend may have better authority, but this is the latest recognized authority on the grain trade of Canada including the port of Montreal.

In reply to the hon. member for Acadia, the total tonnage last year was 9,137,281 tons. I regret I have not the figures here for 1921, but I shall be pleased to supply that information to my hon. friend.
Very well. I wanted the tonnage for the same years as those for which the minister gave the income, so that we can see how the charges are increasing in comparison with the tonnage.
Who fixes the salaries of the harbour commissioners?
The commissioners themselves.
The government have no control whatever?
No control.

I am surprised at the attitude taken by some hon. members on this bill, and I must thank the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George for the support he has given to it. I would think that his opinion, coming as he does from the city of Montreal, but representing the opposing party

in that city, would carry some weight with hon. members on the opposition side. We hear that money is being squandered all over the country, and this is given as an instance of the squandering of money. On the contrary Mr. Chairman, if there is an expenditure we should support it is this one, because we are really not spending any money here at all; we are merely lending the money to the harbour commission of Montreal, and I do not think I am wrong when I say that that is the only harbour commission in the whole country which pays back interest on the money that we lend to it.
And Vancouver.
I like to see Vancouver joining the select circle. I hope the hon. member for Vancouver Centre will support this bill.
Why not let it go through? Why stop it?

If my hon. friends want to carry the vote, certainly I shall not dbject, but I do not want to let my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George stand alone on the other s.ide in supporting this bill, which some* of my friends apposite have been unwise enough to oppose.
Do not obstruct it.

We have the hon. member for South Winnipeg talking about the mixing of grain. I believe he is rather willing to mix things up a little in 'connection with this bill. We could not telll whether he was talking about the present bill or about a bill concerning a bridge projected two years ago. I remember that at that time when we said the leader of the opposition was not very favourable to the project, we were taxed with creating prejudice over that fact. We were told that we did not want to have the leader of the opposition presented in his proper colours before the people of Montreal. Tonight we find not only members from the back benches of the party opposite but even one of the leaders of it taking direct objection to the construction of this bridge in Montreal, pretending that the other bridge would be sufficient to carry all the traffic and that the new bridge is not needed at all. Then the leader of the opposition got up and wanted to know what bridge we were talking of, and my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville very properly remarked that at all events we were not discussing the bridge that was promised by my hon. friends on the other side in the

Canada Evidence Act
Chateauguay by-election, but which was never built, although they carried the seat on that promise at that time.
Coming back to this bill, Mr. Chairman, I am rather surprised when I hear some of our western friends objecting to the lending of money to the harbour of Montreal, a loan on which good interest will be paid. It was only the other day that it was proposed to spend $3,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway, and my hon. friend from 'South Winnipeg then rose, and not only did he think we should spend that amount lof money, but he said that that was not enough, that we should spend more this very year. Then the vote for the Welland canall was called1, amounting to $14,000,000, and he stood there silent, like a statue of alabaster and! had nothing to 'say against that at all. But when it comes to lending money to the harbour of Montreal, on which we will reap good interest every year, he finds all kinds of difficulties. He says we are mixing Canadian grain with American grain, and he mixes this bridge with the other bridge. The bridge has absolutely nothing to do with this loan from the Montreal harbour.

You are buying right of way for the bridge all over. You have spent an enormous sum of money.
Mr. :ST. PERE: The bridge has to land somewhere.

This parliament has decided to build a bridge, and my hon. friend's party were so strongly in favour of it that when we suggested they wrere really objecting to it, they took very strong issue with us on that point, and said that they did not want us to believe that they had the least objection to it at all. But the bridge, Mr. Chairman, is a separate project altogether from the Montreal harbour works. I would also remind my hon. friend that tolls will be collected on that bridge that will help a great deal to meet the interest on the capital investment. But the project we are here considering is the harbour itself, not the bridge. Again, I express my surprise when wei from the eastern part of the country are so willing to support votes of money for works in the west, that hon. gentlemen from the west oppose legislation that proposes, not to spend money, but simply to lend a certain sum, not on an untried experiment, but on a tried harbour-and a loan on which wei shall reap interest for every cent spent.

Preamble agreed to.
Bill reported.
