speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is on
your file of Senate bills.

The bill is Bill X6 from the Senate. It received its third reading and1 was passed by the Senate on June 16th. It wai
Canada Evidence Act

introduced, explained!, and given its first reading in this House on Friday last. When we come to the second section of the bill I can repeat the explanation already given, if hon. members so desire.

The bill1 is practically
the same as the English act.

Absolutely the same, except for one word.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-copies of entries.

The entire bill is embodied in clause 2. It is copied from the English act, which is known in England as the Bankers' Books Evidence Act. The law in Canada has been that in all cases, especially in all criminal cases, the best possible proof available had to be produced, which meant that in all cases where bank books or bank records were required to be produced before the court the original books had to be brought, which caused a great deal of inconvenience to the banks. The bill is being passed at the request of the Canadian Bankers' Association with the object of enabling the bankers to produce duly certified extracts. The bill provides that the extracts shall either be certified to by the oath of the manager or accountant given in open court, or by an affidavit of these official's taken in the usual way. Hon. gentlemen wilil notice that there is a proviso guaranteeing all the rights of litigants and other parties concerned; subsection 3 provides that in any case where, for special cause, the court desires to order the production of the book itself the book shall be produced.
Is the bill a fair transcript of the English act?

It is an absolute transcript except on two points; we have added the words "books or records." Banks sometimes keep their accounts in loose-leaf ledgers and in index cards, and the word "records" has been added to cover these two documents. No provision is made for costs as in the ^English act, because as my hon. friend knows tthe Canada Evidence Act applies to the administration of the Criminal Code and costs are not adjudged in criminal matters. Apart from that, this bill and the English act are identical.	.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. LUCIEN CANNON (Solicitor General) moved that the House go into committee on Bill No. 203, to amend certain provisions of the Criminal Code respecting the possession of weapons.
On section 1-dangerous weapons.
Who will explain this bill? It certainly does not look like the short bill described by the Prime Minister.

The measure looks rather bulky, but it includes both the bill and also the provisions of the Criminal Code which are being amended. The main object of the bill is to replace section 118 of the Criminal Code as it exists to-day. If the section is enacted as provided by this bill it will require a permit for the sale of weapons, the sale of ammunition, the importation of weapons and ammunition, and also the possession of weapons, firearms and ammunition. Secondly, the bill provides for the issuance of the permits by the Department of Justice or by officials designated by that department. Thirdly, it provides for an increase in the penalties imposed for infractions of the act. Certain objections were raised to the original bill as introduced, on the ground that considerable harm might result to that trade from the section covering or including the sporting rifle or arms used for sporting purposes. The act has been amended so that none of these are touched.
Mr. M.ANION:	Is this bill now satisfactory to the dealers in sporting rifles and tha/ sort of thing? I have received a lot of protests from them, although I am not familiar with the question.

I think these objections
have now been withdrawn in view of the amendment introduced. This afternoon I was put in touch with one gentleman who had certain objections to the definition of the word "ammunition," but II suggested an amendment which apparently met his wishes. When we come to that part of the bill I intend to move that amendment.

So far as the minister
understands, the objections raised by the hardware dealers and those who deal in the sale of weapons are met in the bill as it will be amended?

Yes.

Criminal Code
Mr. M-cCLEN AGII AN:	This ball was
objected to by the Hardware Merchants' Association of Canada. Their secretary appeared before the committee and had the clause relating to shot-guns removed. That took 'away a great deal of the objection that had been raised by the dealers. They do not objedt to the placing of restrictions upon the carrying of concealed weapons, 'but they showed the committee that Canada was a great sporting country, and to put any restrictions on the dealers and on the men using firearms and rifles would injure our tourist trade. But after this amendment had been made the original bill was introduced here, though I think it should have gone to the Private Bills committee in order that the matter might be thoroughly discussed. We have a provision with reference to ammunition which puts it back in its original shape, because when you buy ammunition for a rifle the same ammunition can be used in a revolver. The ammunition for a 22-calibre rifle can be used in a 22-calibre revolver, and the same with rifles and revolvers of other calibres; the ammunition is interchangeable. We claim you cannot make any amendment to that ammunition clause; the only thing is to withdraw it. Then you have your restriction against your firearms such as revolvers and pistols, but say nothing about ammunition, which, as I say, is interchangeable. A dealer is liable to a fine of
SI,000	and two years' imprisonment if he violates the provisions of a certain clause in the bill. There is also a clause under which a man who obtained a permit in Ottawa and went down to Rockland with the ammunition would be fined because he would be in the county of Russell. It is all mixed up. In the interests of sport in this country we should remove this restriction. The bill should have gone to the Private Bills committee where it could be discussed with more freedom.
I have not heard a good reason why an innocent man can be sent to gaol for two years.
He cannot.
Why not?
The hon. member for Ottawa has just explained that in the original bill arms used for sporting purposes were apparently included, but the bill as drafted now, as my hon. friend will read-
Your hon. friend has had no chance to read it.

In paragraph 2 of clause 1, under the subparagraphs (a), (i), (ii), (iii),
(iv) and (v), the different kinds of firearms covered by the bill are enumerated. If my hon. friend reads these clauses I think he will come to the conclusion that the sporting community is in no way affected. In answer to the objection raised by my hon. friend from Ottawa concerning ammunition, I intended, in order to meet the objection raised, to amend the bill. The word "ammunition" is defined in paragraph (c) at the top of page 2 as follows:
''Ammunition'' means all amimuniition that can be used with a weapon.
And the word "weapon" would be interpreted in accordance with its definition under paragraph (b). But as the hon. member for Ottawa mentioned, the same ammunition might be used both for sporting arms and for arms which are enumerated and prohibited under this act. So that I intended amending the definition of ammunition by saying that ammunition would mean ammunition for use exclusively with any weapon to which subsection 2 of this section applies. If the bill is amended in that way the objection raised by my hon. friend would be met.
I understand the bill was introduced in the Senate?
Yes.
Would this not be the time to reciprocate and throw out some of the Senate measures?

I do not think any good purpose can be served by worrying over that word "ammunition." So far as the bill refers to revolvers and pistols I am in hearty agreement. Long ago before I came to parliament, I thought that if ever I came here I would introduce a measure dealing with revolvers and pistols. In the main the revolver is a useless weapon for any law-abiding person. I do not think this bill should trouble itself about ammunition at all. I do not care what definition you give to ammunition, you cannot meet the needs of the case because ammunition which is used in revolvers can also be used in smaller rifles and some of the larger ones as well. Therefore I do not think any definition you can give to ammunition will get you over the difficulty. Why ' should we not fix our attention entirely on the weapon and then the ammunition will take care of itself? As regards the other things in this bill that are spoken of as dangerous weapons, I fully appreciate the dangers that might arise from carrying concealed weapons; but the difficulty of guarding
Criminal Code

against them seems to me so vast that I hesitate to approach it. It is distinctly stated that the weapons which a person must not have in his possession are:
Any sword, sword -.blade, bayonet, .pike, pike-head, spear, spear-head, dirk, dagger, stiletto, or any similar device or contrivance.
These are dangerous looking weapons, but ,1 usually carry in my pocket a big jack-knife that on occasion icould be just as dangerous ,a weapon as one of these. I have lying around at home an old bayonet which according to this bill I would be forbidden to keep. Nevertheless, while I might have to .discard that particular weapon, if I wanted to make a weapon for murderous purposes I could go into blacksmith's shop and in half an hour I could turn out just as dangerous a weapon as this bayonet or any of the weapons referred to in the bill. I mention that simply as an illustration of the difficulty that confronts us in dealing with the question in this way. A good big butcher-knife that every farmer has around his farm might be just as dangerous a weapon in the hands of a man who is murderously inclined as any one of the weapons mentioned in the bill. I am inclined to think that in this particular matter of dealing with dangerous weapons we had better make haste very slowly, deal with the revolvers and let the ammunition take care of itself. While the other weapons may be dangerous, the difficulty of meeting the situation seems to be so great that if we pass this measure as it now stands we shall only land ourselves in trouble and possibly subject honest people, people who are not murderously disposed at all, to a great deal of annoyance by an over-zealous official.
I may assure my hon. friend that he can still keep possession of the arms that he has mentioned, because his case is provided for in subsection (3) paragraph (g).
I saw that.

I should be very sorry if we had to remove any arms from my hon. friend.
Mr. kORKE: I had no idea my desk-mate carried such dangerous weapons around with him. I am going to keep an eye on him from now on.

I remember some years ago a bill similar to this came up in the House when the Hon. Mr. Doherty was Minister of Justice. At that time the present Solicitor

General, if I remember rightly, took exception to some of the weapons named in this bill. He asked, if I remember aright, who wanted to barter with a cannon or who would go around concealing a cannon. I remember on that same occasion asking the then Prime Minister if it was his intention to have children go to the Minister of Justice for a permit to have a child's air-gun. I thought at the time it was a ridiculous provision and I think so to-day.

It is getting
worse now.

There is another feature of this. W'e have really omitted weapons which are possibly far more dangerous than these obsolete swords, bayonets, spear-heads, dirks and daggers. There is such a thing, if I remember reading the history of our criminal activities, as a sawed-off shot-gun. This is far more dangerous in a riot or la hold-up than any of the weapons mentioned in this bill and we seem to have omitted it altogether. I agree a good deal with the hon. member for Lisgar. Let us, if we wish to restrict the use of these weapons, confine ourselves to those which we can restrict and not endeavour to give a long enumeration making crimes which we shall never be able to detect.

I rise to protest as I
have many times in this House against this eternal restriction of the liberties of the Canadian people. I remember quite well the incident referred to by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) concerning the Solicitor General's attitude at that time. I would like also to impress upon him that there are in. this country thousands and tens of thousands of war souvenirs which have been brought home by the returned soldiers and which I think come under the restrictive clauses of this bill. At least I would like to ask him if they do or do not. It is time this parliament stopped placing restrictions upon the liberties of the Canadian people. We are not a band of outlaws and we should be trusted to some extent.

I should think
the Solicitor General would like to revert to that former position which he took so strongly and so well. Does he not feel like doing so? If he does not want to revert to that former position which has been so highly praised in both quarters of the House, why does he not at least make this bill something that is going to work? Let him cover the sawed-off shot-gun which is certainly much more dangerous than any of these old pikes, or

National Railways and Shipping
bayonets, or dirks, or other things described in the bill. The sawed-off shot-gun and the revolver are the two things which are really dangerous. Cannot we get this bill down to something which everybody will understand at once and which any police officer can enforce?

Would the Solicitor
General be good enough to answer my question?

I would like to explain
first that with myself las well as with others, responsibility of office always gives maturity of thought. I am sure the hon. member for Quebec South will realize that quite soon himself. As to the returned men having arms in their possession, I do not think this bill would prevent them from having them.
I would refer my hon. friend who has raised that question to subsection (3) paragraph (g) of the bill which I think will cover the case.

If the weapons are not obsolete it does not cover them. I have in my possession a sword which happened to belong to one of my ancestors. It is not obsolete in any way. It is really an excellent sword and it probably could not be manufactured now.
Has it ever been used?

Yes, in service. It is not
obsolete; I would have to put it in the melting pot if this bill goes through. I have some other war souvenirs that would also have to go into the melting pot. It does not help me by way of defence to say they are not usable, because they are.

This bill was introduced

Mr. Speaker, I move that the bill be referred to the committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.

The committee has
